p.seg: Nineteen Poems Presented to My Elder Brother Xiùcai Gōngmù Upon His Joining the Army
Nineteen Poems Presented to My Elder Brother Xiùcai Gōngmù Upon His Joining the Army
A pair of phoenixes conceal their radiant light,
Tucking wings atop Tàishān's cliffs.
Raising heads, they sip the morning dew,
Basking in sunlight, preening their plumes.
Long calls echo as they play among clouds,
At times descending to rest by orchid ponds.
They deem themselves beyond worldly dust,
Their purity eternal, never to fade.
How could they foresee life's hardships?
Hunters come with suspicions toward us.
Cloud-like nets block the four directions,
High snares spread in disarray.
Swift flight hindered by circumstance,
Six wings find no room to spread.
Noble forms submit to long reins,
Finally bound by the times' constraints.
A lone male turns to solitary flight,
Mournful cries lament this living separation.
Pacing, he lingers with his beloved mate,
Passionate sighs echo through mountain slopes.
When birds are gone, good bows are stored;
Plans exhausted, one stands imperiled.
Though fortune and misfortune lie within oneself,
The world's path is fraught with peril.
How can I return to my humble attire,
Holding jade, treasuring six wonders?
Roaming carefree in the great void,
Hand in hand, forever together.
The mandarin ducks in flight,
Rustling are their wings.
By morning they roam the high plains,
By evening rest on orchid isles.
Harmoniously they sing in unison,
Glancing back at their companions,
Bowing and rising with deep emotion,
Leisurely and at ease.
The mandarin ducks in flight,
Call out to mates, summon friends.
By morning they roam the high plains,
By evening rest mid-stream isles.
Neck to neck, wings aflutter,
Serenely floating on clear currents.
Nibbling on orchid and iris,
Bowing and rising, free and untroubled.
I swim across that long river,
And rest upon its bank;
I climb that high ridge,
And cut its thorny brush.
Alas, my journey forward,
Walking alone, solitary and slow.
Gazing up at the soothing south wind,
Tears fall like rain!
I swim across that long river,
And rest upon its shore;
I climb that high ridge,
And cut its wolfberry twigs.
Alas, my solitary march,
With none to look to, none to rely on.
Gazing up at the soothing south wind,
I sit and rise, restless.
Gentle, kind breezes,
Sweep away the light dust;
Glistening white waves,
Swirl with swimming fish.
As for my toils,
They hold thoughts of a beloved.
Awake, I speak and long ponder,
My heart fixed on my dear one.
Where is my dear one now?
He has left me, traveling far.
Abandoning these fragrant herbs,
To wear common mugwort and wormwood.
Though said to be remote and deep,
How can there be no hardship?
Thinking of my noble man,
How could he be free from harm?
Human life is brief,
Heaven and earth endure long.
A span of a hundred years,
Who can call it long-lived?
I long to ascend as an immortal,
To achieve undying fame.
Holding the reins, I hesitate,
Looking up to my friend.
Where has my friend gone?
Beyond these hills and ridges.
Who says the river is wide?
A reed could sail across.
Yet I regret this eternal parting,
That road stretches far away.
Gazing, I cannot reach him,
Pacing back and forth, lost and unsure.
The fine steed is already trained,
The splendid robes gleam.
Left hand grasps the Fánruò bow,
Right hand holds the Wàngguī arrows.
Like wind and lightning he speeds,
Treading on shadows, chasing flight.
Sweeping across the central plains,
His glances full of grace.
With my beloved companion,
I mount the light carriage,
Crossing southern long mounds,
Passing northern clear streams.
Aiming high, startling geese in flight,
Dipping low, luring fish from depths,
Engaged in hunting excursions,
Such joy, such delight!
Ascending high, gazing afar,
Looking up and down, I sigh.
I lament this hidden bondage,
And the distant, lengthy road.
Though I have fine music,
Who will sing clear songs with me?
Though I have fair features,
Who will make them bloom?
Looking up, I question the high clouds,
Looking down, I entrust to light waves.
Riding the currents to flee far away,
Holding regrets by the mountain's curve.
The light carriage speeds swiftly,
Resting in that vast forest.
Spring trees burst with blossoms,
Spreading leaves, casting shade.
Soft valley winds whisper,
Stirring my plain qín's strings.
Bright yellow birds chirp,
Turning to mates, playing with notes.
Moved, my feelings race,
Longing for the one I admire.
My heart is filled with sorrow,
Eternal whistles, long chants.
Vast, mighty rivers,
Encircle our capital's lands;
Lush, green woods,
Bloom brilliantly, radiating light.
Fish and dragons frolic in water,
Mountain birds flock in flight.
I harness the carriage for an outing,
Forgetting return as dusk falls.
Thinking of my good friend,
Like thirst, like hunger.
My wishes remain unfulfilled,
How sorrowful, how sad!
Resting followers in orchid fields,
Grazing horses on Huàshān.
Casting lines over flat marshes,
Dangling hooks in long streams.
Eyes follow returning geese,
Hands strum the five-stringed lute.
At ease in every gesture,
My mind wanders in the great mystery.
I praise that old angler,
Who, catching fish, forgets the trap.
The Yǐng craftsman is gone;
To whom can I speak fully?
In the quiet, clear night,
The bright moon shines through the window.
A gentle breeze stirs my robe,
The curtained canopy raised high.
Fine wine fills the cup,
But none to share the joy.
Lute and zither lie ready,
But who will play them with me?
I admire those of like mind,
Their fragrance like orchids.
The beloved is no longer here;
How can I not sigh forever!
Riding the wind, roaming high,
Far ascending divine peaks.
Befriending Sōng and Qiáo,
Hand in hand, traveling together.
At dawn, we depart from Tàihuà,
By dusk, rest in the divine land.
Strumming the qín, chanting poems,
To briefly forget sorrow.
Qín and poems bring their own joy,
Far journeys are to be treasured.
Embracing the Way, I go alone,
Abandoning wisdom, forgetting self.
Silent and unburdened,
What do I seek from others?
Long dwelling on sacred peaks,
Nourishing my will, cultivating my spirit.
The vulgar world is hard to enlighten,
Chasing after things without return.
The sage sees far,
Returning to the natural way.
All things are one,
The four seas share one home.
Sharing it with others,
What have I to regret?
Life is like a fleeting sojourn,
Briefly seen, then suddenly ends.
Worldly affairs are chaotic,
Abandon eight-tenths of them.
Though the marsh pheasant hungers,
It desires not the garden grove.
How can it submit to service,
Toiling body and troubling heart?
The body is noble, fame is base,
Wherein lie glory and disgrace?
Precious is fulfilling one's will,
Following the heart without regret.
A Poem of Hidden Resentment
Alas, I am lightly blessed,
In youth met with misfortune.
Lonely and unaware,
Still in swaddling clothes.
Mother and brother reared me,
With kindness, not sternness.
Relying on love, I was indulged,
Without discipline or teacher.
When I reached capping age,
I relied on favor and let loose.
My heart aspired to antiquity,
Following what I esteemed.
I embraced Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ,
Valuing the self, disdaining things.
Aiming to preserve simplicity,
Nourishing plainness, keeping truth whole.
I am not clever,
And fond of the obscure.
Like Zǐyù's failures,
I repeatedly added to the dust.
The great contain broadly,
Holding filth and shame.
The people are often perverse,
Governance not from oneself.
With this narrow heart,
I clearly showed right and wrong.
Awakened, I reflect on faults,
Painful as fresh wounds.
Wishing to lessen my errors,
Slander and criticism boiled.
My nature harms none,
Yet often incurs hatred.
Once ashamed before Liǔ Xiàhuì,
Now shamed by Sūn Dēng.
Within, I betray my longtime heart,
Without, I shame good friends.
I admire Yán Jūnpíng and Zhèng Zǐzhēn,
Who delighted in the Way, living in leisure.
Uninvolved with the world,
Spirit and energy serene.
Alas, I am unblessed,
Burdened with many troubles.
Not sent from heaven,
But truly from my stubborn neglect.
Reason fails, troubles knot,
Finally leading to prison.
Facing base interrogations,
Confined in this secluded barrier.
Truly ashamed to plead innocence,
The times are not with me.
Though I claim righteousness and honesty,
My spirit is shamed, will broken.
Washing in the blue waves,
How can it mend this?
Honking wild geese,
Flap wings northward.
Moving with the season,
Finding joy, forgetting sorrow.
Alas, my indignant sigh,
Cannot match them.
Things counter to wishes,
Meet with this delay.
Poverty and success are fated,
What more to seek?
The ancients had a saying,
Goodness avoids fame.
Follow times, be reverent and silent,
Blame and regret won't arise.
Wàn Shí was circumspect,
Securing family, preserving honor.
Worldly affairs are chaotic,
They only disturb my feelings.
In peace, be cautious,
Thus ends in advantage and steadfastness.
Glorious spirit fungus,
Blooms thrice a year.
Why alone am I,
With aims unfulfilled?
Chastened by hardship, I think of return,
In heart, deep remorse.
Hoping to strive in future,
Scentless, soundless.
Gathering ferns on mountain slopes,
Loosening hair in rock caves.
Eternally whistling, long chanting,
Nourishing nature, prolonging life.
Two Poems of Expressing Aspirations
The hidden dragon nurtures divine form,
Washing scales, playing in orchid pond.
Craning neck, admiring the Great Hall,
Resting feet, awaiting Huángxī.
Auspicious clouds not yet casting shadows,
Lingering by the sunny slope.
The distant are not my match,
Who would conform to vulgar ways?
Different kinds hard to fully align,
Base opinions scatter wildly.
Bumpy road brings regret,
Noble aims cannot be applied.
Plowing moved Nìng Yuè,
Mat straw inspired Zhāng Yí.
I shall leave the crowd,
Staff in hand, follow Hóngyá.
The roc shakes six wings,
How can the netter ensnare it?
Floating in the great void,
Seeking new companions.
Wing to wing, soaring the Milky Way,
Drinking dew, feeding on jade branches.
Often thinking of worldly people,
Rushing at dawn in carriages.
Tranquility attains the natural,
What use is glory and splendor?
The quail boasts in wormwood groves,
Looking up, laughs at the divine phoenix's flight.
The well is home to tadpoles,
Where can the sacred turtle return?
I regret my clumsiness in life,
Freely thinking long thoughts.
Truly distant, unlike the world,
Righteous fame not what I seek.
Past deeds were already mistaken,
The future can still be pursued.
Why in human affairs,
Let my heart be unsettled?
Passionately thinking of ancients,
Dreaming of their radiant faces.
Wishing to meet a kindred spirit,
Venting feelings, revealing subtleties.
Caves hide many recluses,
Rising lightly, I seek my teacher.
At dawn, climb Jīshān's peak,
By dusk, unaware of hunger.
In dark abode, nourish soul,
For millennia, ever peaceful.
A Poem of Roaming Immortals
Gazing afar at pines on the mountain,
Lush and green in deep valleys.
How lofty they stand alone,
Peerless in independence.
I long to wander beneath them,
But the path is utterly blocked.
Wáng Qiáo has left me,
Riding clouds, driving six dragons.
Floating, playing in Xuānpǔ,
Meeting Huángdì and Lǎozǐ on the way.
They taught me the natural Way,
Vast, like enlightening a child.
Gathering herbs at Zhōngshān's corner,
Taking them, my appearance changed.
Molting, discarding filth and burdens,
Making friends, dwelling at Bǎntóng.
Facing wine, playing the Nine Sháos,
Elegant songs, how harmonious!
Long parted from common folk,
Who can glimpse their traces?
Six-Character Poems, Ten Pieces
Six-Character Poems, Ten Pieces
Only in high antiquity, Yáo and Shùn,
Two men's virtues equal and even,
Not using the world for private kin.
Noble, simple, kind and obedient,
They saved and aided the masses of the four seas.
In the era of Táng and Yú, order prevailed,
All states revered kinship, without strife,
Wise and foolish each fulfilled their wills.
Peaceful, joyful, forgetting inner cares,
Excellent indeed, those times were delightful.
When wisdom is used for artificial action,
Laws multiply, breeding bandits in reaction,
Chaos summons chaos without cessation.
The great man dwells in dark silence, voiceless,
Calming all with stillness, self-corrected.
Which is dearer: fame or one's own life?
Alas! The worldly chase glory in strife.
Racing and striving, exhausting essence and vigor,
Gains and losses entangle, worry and fear trigger,
Hence toil and unrest become their figure.
Excessive pursuit of life invites blame,
A hall full of gold and jade none can claim.
The ancients embraced this coarse and plain,
Alone making virtue their companion,
Thus prolonging their days, imperishable in union.
Fame and prominence breed increasing woes,
High position and power sow disaster's roots,
Beauty harms nature, beyond all doubts.
Rich flavors are like poison, hard to cure,
Why do the greedy not think and ensure?
Dōngfāng Shuò was of utmost purity,
Outwardly seeming corrupt, inwardly chaste,
Defiling himself, witty, hiding his name in haste.
Unentangled by worldly burdens,
His desires unmet, yet he sought no gains.
Chǔ's Zǐwén excelled in office,
Thrice as prime minister, without delight,
Liǔxià lowered himself, enduring shame's blight.
Not treating rank and salary as their own,
Quiet and reverent, only these two were known.
Lǎo Lái's wife, wise and famed,
Unwilling for her husband to serve Jīng,
Together they fled office to farm in hiding.
Joyful in the Way, leisurely gathering duckweed,
She maintained high virtue, never to recede.
Alas, the ancient worthy Yuán Xiàn,
Abandoned rich fare and rosy complexion,
Delighting in frequent emptiness, hunger, and dejection.
Humble in form, relaxed in body, broad in mind,
Content in his time, without worries to find.

Wealth, honor, and glory,

What the ancients feared,
Grand houses that bring harm.
People harm those above,
Beasts detest the net's snare.

In song, it is said,

Poverty and lowliness are easy to bear,

Toil with humility, few regrets to own,

Forceful ways bring disaster,
Much action invites woes.
To gain peace and joy,

Those who strain their spirit wear out,

Yán Huí died young,
And down to child Wū.
Those who indulge their bodies in excess,
None fail to perish early.
What are wine and beauty?
Now they bring their own guilt.
In song, it is said,
Wine and beauty make one wither.

Abandon sageliness and discard learning,
Let the mind wander in dark silence.
Regretting past errors,
One should not seek gain.
Fishing in a single stream,
Finding joy in one land.
With hair unbound, singing aloud,
Responders fill the surroundings.
In song, it is said,
Let the mind wander in dark silence.

I long to be with Wáng Qiáo,
Riding clouds to roam the eight extremes.
Soaring over the five peaks,
Swiftly traveling myriad miles.
He grants me divine medicine,
Spontaneous wings grow from my sides.
Breathing the great harmony,
Refining my form, changing my appearance.
In song, it is said,
I long to roam the eight extremes.
Wandering around Zhōngshān,
Resting my carriage at layered walls.
Wandering around Zhōngshān,
Resting my carriage at layered walls.
Above, shaded by a jeweled canopy,
Below, picking radiant flowers.
Receiving the Way from Queen Mother,
Then ascending to the purple court.
Roaming freely in the celestial paths,
Living a thousand years in eternal life.
In song, it is said,
Wandering at the layered walls.
A Poem Longing for Family
What can I do with sorrow? Sorrow is endless,
Constant grief, my heart feels torn.
What to do with sorrow? Sad thoughts abound,
Emotions knotted, impossible to unwind.
Suddenly losing support, alone and desolate,
Mourning inwardly, I cry without sound.
Longing to repay kindness, now far beyond reach,
Feeling the care I received, my heart breaks.
Alas, mother and brother, forever hidden away,
Recalling their forms, inwardly crushed with pain!
Moved by spring, I think of my kind mother,
Wishing to see her once, but no path leads there.
Gazing at the southern mountains, I sigh in grief,
Touched by the staff, tears flow like streams.
Remembering past days when mother and brother were here,
My heart was joyful, life spanned the world.
Suddenly gone, beyond pursuit,
My heart in poverty, only sorrow remains.
Entering the empty hall, vast and unsupported,
Seeing left-behind objects, my heart shatters.
In the midnight sadness, whom can I tell?
Alone, wiping tears, holding grief and woe.
As days pass far away, my heart yearns,
Longing for my parents, tears unrestrained.
With my kind mother gone, who will cherish me?
Looking at myself, my heart aches deeply.
Pleading to the blue heavens, but heaven does not hear,
Tears fall like rain, sighing at the blue clouds.
Wanting to cast off sorrow, but it returns,
Pain so profound, impossible to sever.
In Reply to the Two Guos, Three Poems
Under heaven, the restless masses,
From lower capital to upper capital they rush.
The two Guos, extraordinary in thought,
Transcendently came northward in campaign.
Finding joy in the Way, lodging in a humble hut,
Noble ambitions free from worldly schemes.
In good time, their wishes met,
Thus forming bonds of joyful affection.
Gentlemen value righteousness as kin,
Kindness and friendship steadfast for life.
Lack of resolve brings self-made disaster,
Repeatedly causing conflicts to arise.
Yùzǐ hid by the bridge,
Niè Zhèng altered his form.
Reflecting on this, I feel fear and alarm,
Concerned only to secure my own peace.
Now I must dwell in another land,
My stern carriage cannot delay.
Originally hoping for lasting harmony,
Now unable to be together again.
The two gifted me with fine poems,
Fragrant as secluded orchids' scent.
Longing for home, thinking of my dear ones,
How can I not be filled with indignant emotion?
In the past, blessed by my father and brothers' grace,
I was spared heavy burdens in my youthful days.
Through neglect, I grew accustomed to idleness,
Hiding my tracks by the northern mountainside.
I only wish to nurture my life's essence,
To the end, I seek nothing else.
But fine days do not await my will,
In my prime, I faced a world of turmoil.
Stumbling, I followed the world's teachings,
Often fearing to be caught in its snares.
Fúxī and Shénnóng are far, far gone,
I beat my breast and sigh alone.
The northern rule values tolerance,
The fisherman loves to stir the waves.
Though carefree, it is also hard—
Not what my heart admires.
Better to soar beyond this realm,
Feast on jade, rinse with morning rays.
Cast aside worldly things and base burdens,
Roam freely in the great harmony.
Gather friends on sacred peaks,
Play the qin, sing clear songs.
If there are those who can follow this path,
What need to praise the ancients?
Closely observing worldly affairs,
Perils and worries abound.
Favors and repayments are traded like goods,
The great Way hides, no longer revealed.
Thorny brambles block the peaceful road—
How can one stroll safely forward?
Cunning and wisdom contend for power,
Fame and rank are not fit to hold.
The luan and phoenix avoid trapping nets,
Fleeing far to the Kūnlún wilds.
Zhuāng Zhōu mourned the divine turtle,
Yuè Jī sighed for the king's carriage.
The perfected man preserves himself within,
Embracing simplicity, delighting in mystery.
Why sacrifice for merit and fame,
Only to be listed in records?
Such are my clear preferences,
As Yáng Shì sighed at the crossroads.
I'll go my way, following my heart,
Daring to decline paths not aligned.
For Ruǎn Dérú, One Poem
For Ruǎn Dérú, One Poem
Bearing sorrow, I return to my old home,
Deeply moved, my heart and liver ache.
In good times, I met a few like you,
Our talks consoled, fragrant as orchids.
I once regretted not knowing you sooner,
But meeting felt like old joy renewed.
Never thought we'd part so suddenly—
Separated, I sigh in sorrow.
Nothing in life stays unchanged,
Parting is easy, meeting again is hard.
The Yǐng craftsman is gone,
Artisan Shí rests silent now.
The marsh pheasant thrives on wild grasses,
The divine turtle enjoys muddy seclusion.
Glorious fame defiles the person,
High positions bring many disasters.
Better to cast off external burdens,
Follow one's will, nurture vast energy.
Yán Huì admired Yǒuyú's era,
Xí Zǐ yearned for Huángdì and Xuānyuán;
Who were Juān and Péng alone,
But those who found peace in their aims?
Indulging in near desires,
Once gone, they cannot be reclaimed.
Life's essence gathers through preparation,
Don't ease your mind with mere caution.
The southern lands are dry and not cool,
Plan early and complete your tasks.
May you cherish your virtuous nature,
On the road, beware wind and cold.
I strive to express what I feel,
Writing this, my heart aches with sorrow.
Seven Poems from a Wine Gathering
Seven Poems from a Wine Gathering
How joyful, wandering in the garden,
Viewing endlessly all around.
A hundred flowers bloom with fragrance,
Towering terraces stand lofty and far.
Trees and woods intertwine chaotically,
In dark ponds, bream and carp play.
Light pellets bring down soaring birds,
Fine lines catch sturgeon and perch.
Seated, we offer fine praises,
Different breaths, yet one harmonious tune.
By the stream, we present clear wine,
Soft songs flow from white teeth.
The plain qin plays elegant tunes,
Clear notes rise with the wind.
Is this gathering not joyful?
Yet I regret Dōngyě Zǐ is not here.
In wine, I think of the recluse,
Holding to the old way, start to end.
But let me feel the seven strings,
Entrust my heart to a knowing friend.
Gentle, gentle flowing water,
Drifting away, wave on wave;
Floating, floating cypress boat,
Now buoyant, now delayed.
A soft whistle in the clear breeze,
Paddling leisurely, swaying along.
Set aside oars, cast the fishing rod,
Pass the year in carefree ease.
Lovely are those mandarin ducks,
Folding wings as they swim.
Pecking down at green algae,
Finding shelter in the vast flow.
Soaring over white rapids at dawn,
Resting on divine isles at dusk.
Swaying on clear waves,
Rising and sinking with them.
Among algae, by orchid ponds,
Harmonious sounds stir the air.
Strumming the clear shāng mode,
My mind roams the great form.
Devoting myself to cultivate virtue,
Leaving behind kind echoes of music.
Since Zhōng Zǐqī is no more,
Who appreciates my aspirations?
I put away the strings, disperse my thoughts,
Wander and fish in the ninefold depths.
Torrents fall from a thousand ren,
Some baited hooks hang suspended.
How sublime, Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
Dwelling in peace for eternal years.
Truly, this is the dragon's transformation,
Cleansing the will, vast and boundless.
Soughing, soughing, the cool wind,
Born where the river banks divide.
Turning away from lush woods,
Looking down at the crimson shore.
Embracing sunlight, breathing forth blossoms,
Treading frost, yet never fading.
Alas, my perspective differs—
All flowers wither around me.
My heart is burdened with sorrow,
Who understands the profound mystery?
Lush, lush, orchid clusters,
Planted in the central plains.
Green leaves, deep and abundant,
Lovely petals, thick and full.
Rich, rich, the orchid's fragrance,
Carried by the wind, far and wide.
Destined for the pepper-scented chambers,
Spreading perfume in the dragon hall.
Gazing at those autumn grasses,
I sigh, alas, and feel the loss.
One Miscellaneous Poem
A light breeze fans clear air,
Clouds disperse in all directions.
Bright, bright, the shining moon,
Glorious at the high corner.
I urge the noble youth,
To join hands, share the carriage.
Dragon-steeds, wings outspread,
Raising bits, pacing slowly.
Solemn, we journey by night,
To reach my friend's abode.
Lamplight radiates brilliance,
Colorful curtains stretched long.
Phoenix cups pour sweet wine,
Divine cauldrons cook fine fish.
Strings surpass Zǐyě's skill,
Laments outdo Mián Jū's art.
Chanting of the great simplicity,
Praising the profound mystery below.
Who can match such talent?
With you, I'd share the tally.
Rhapsody on the Qin, with Preface
From youth I loved music,
and in maturity I have savored it.
I believe all things have their seasons of flourish and decline,
yet this remains unchanged;
flavors may grow tiresome,
but this never wearies.
It can guide and nurture the spirit and energy,
harmonize and express emotions and aspirations.
For dwelling in solitude without melancholy,
nothing compares to music.
Thus, if repeating it is not enough,
one chants to express the will;
if chanting is not enough,

However, instruments of all kinds,

Praising their forms,
their elegance is invariably inherited;
extolling their substance,
hardship and bitterness are esteemed;
depicting their sounds,

admiring their transformative power,
moving listeners to tears is valued.
Beautiful they may be,
yet they do not fully capture the principle.
Examining their origins,
it seems they fundamentally misunderstand music;
considering their intent,
they also fail to grasp the essence of ritual and music.
Among all instruments,
the virtue of the qin is supreme.
Therefore, I compile my thoughts,
to compose a rhapsody for it.
The verses say:
The paulownia tree grows,
upon the lofty peaks of majestic mountains.
Breaking through layered soil to emerge,
it reaches for the celestial pole, soaring high.
Imbued with the pure harmony of heaven and earth,
it absorbs the glorious light of the sun and moon.
Lush and luxuriant in its solitary splendor,
it sends its blossoms flying into the vast sky.
At dusk, it gathers shadows from Yūyuān,

After millennia awaiting its worth,

Moreover, its mountainous terrain,
winds deep and hidden,
rugged and towering.
Peaks interlock, cliffs sheer,
jagged and precipitous.
Crimson bluffs perilous,
green walls ten thousand fathoms high.
Where layered ridges rise,

Vast, lofty, and immensely grand,
they stand majestic and uniquely elegant.
Vapors rise, spreading clouds,
from divine springs, streams gush forth.
Then turbulent waves surge,
wildly rushing in competing currents.
Striking rocks and winding bends,
they roar with pent-up fury.
Surging and churning,
whipping foam and raising waves.
Rushing and roaring,
twisting and intertwining.
Unleashed into the great river,
they cross the central plains.
Calmly turning, slowly flowing,
silently drifting afar.
Vast and expansive,
encircling the hills.
Observe in detail the region's nurtured produce,
the treasures cultivated in its profound depths.
Rare gems and lánggān,
yáo and jǐn radiantly splendid.
Clustered and piled,
abundantly spread around.
To the east, spring orchids bloom,
to the west, shātáng trees grow.
Juān Zǐ dwells on its south,
jade springs bubble before it.
Dark clouds shade above,
soaring phoenixes gather on its summit.
Pure dew moistens its skin,
gentle breezes flow through.
Reverently serene and tranquil,
intimately subtle and leisurely.
What thrives around it,
is naturally divine and beautiful,
fulfilling all thoughts and desires with joy.
Thus, recluses of past eras,
like Róng Qī and Qǐ Jì and their kind,
together climb flying bridges,
cross deep gorges;
grasp jade branches,
ascend steep cliffs;
to wander beneath it.
Gazing afar in all directions,
as if soaring through the skies.
Glancing sideways at Kūnlún,
looking down upon the sea's edge.
Pointing to distant Cāngwú,
facing the winding river's bends.
Awakening to worldly burdens,
they admire the lingering glory of Jīshān.
Envying this mountain's grandeur,
their hearts stirred, they forget to return.
Emotions unbound, they gaze into the distance,
connecting with Xuānyuán's legacy of music.
Admiring Lǎo Tóng in Guīyú,
revering Tài Róng's lofty chants.
Regarding this paulownia, inspiration arises,
thinking to borrow it to convey the heart.
So they cut a sun branch,
measure its suitability;
the sage expresses his thoughts,
crafting an elegant qin.
Then Lí Zǐ oversees the marking,
Jiàng Shī wields the axe;
Kuí and Xiāng offer methods,
Bān and Chuí unleash their genius.
Carving joints and fitting parts,
balanced in density and tone.
Ornate carvings and embellishments,
adorned with patterns and inscriptions.
Inlaid with rhinoceros and ivory,
set with kingfisher green.
Strung with Yuán Kè's silk,
markers of Zhōngshān's jade.
There are images of dragon and phoenix,
forms of ancient figures,
Bó Yá raising his hand,
Zhōng Qǐ listening to the sounds.
Brilliant and radiant,
emitting splendor and brightness.
How exquisite it is!
Líng Lún comparing pitches,
Tián Lián tuning the strings.
Presented to noblemen,
the new melodies clear and bright.
How magnificent!
When first tuned,
jiǎo and yǔ notes arise together,
gōng and zhǐ affirming each other.
Multiple tones emerge in unison,
high and low responding in layers,
leaping and robust,
beautiful sounds about to flourish.
Truly harmonious and utterly captivating.
Then, rectifying the proper tones,
performing exquisite melodies;
playing "White Snow,"
sounding "Clear Jiǎo."
Profusely flowing and shimmering,
abundantly rich and lush.
Brilliantly soaring high,
swiftly following in succession.
Vigorously vying in forward rush,
brilliantly resplendent and intricate.
Shaped like towering mountains,
or resembling flowing waves,
vast and surging,
majestic and lofty.
Restless and aggrieved,
winding and graceful.
Soaring and spreading freely,
cascading and blossoming.
Composing oneself, keeping rhythm,
adapting to changes with measure.
Competing in fame, mastering the art,
moving steadily on course.
Expansive and practiced,
its splendid fame spreads far.
With evident charm it sees off the end,
its lingering echoes drift in the primal essence.
In lofty pavilions and soaring towers,
spacious halls and quiet rooms,
on serene winter nights,
under the bright moon's glow.
Fresh robes emerald bright,
sashes and insignia wafting fragrance.
Thus the instrument's strings were tuned to perfection,
with a tranquil heart and nimble hands.
Every touch and pluck followed the will,
guided solely by intention.
It began with "Lǜ Shuǐ,"
then played the pure "Qīng Zhǐ."
Elegantly evoking Táng Yáo's era,
and concluding with the ode to Wēizǐ.
Broad and bright, profound and smooth,
leisurely and poised in stance.
Strumming the strings, singing calmly,
new melodies arose in succession.
The song went:
"Riding the whirlwind, I rest on Yíngzhōu,
inviting Lièzǐ to be my fine companion.
Feasting on night mist, girded with morning clouds,
soaring lightly, roaming near the heavens.
Harmonizing all things, transcending to self-content,
entrusting fate, accepting departure or stay.
Stirring pure notes to join the gathering,
how entwined are the strings and songs!"
As the melody drew to a close,
all sounds were about to cease.
Changing the tune and mode,
a wondrous performance then unfolded.
Lifting a gentle countenance,
baring fair wrists;
flying slender fingers in swift motion,
a cascade of rapid, flowing notes.
Sometimes lingering with fond looks,
holding back, pressing softly;
lingering to nurture the sound,
composed and savoring its mystery.
Suddenly bursting forth with vigor,
like wind startling, clouds scattering;
desolate yet fierce,
spreading and half-dispersing.
Lush and radiant, scattering widely,
brilliant and dazzling in splendor;
heroic tones soaring high,
resplendent and shining bright.
At times, interlaced sounds mingled,
as if deceptively converging;
dual beauties advancing together,
racing side by side, driving like wings.
At first seeming to diverge,
but ultimately uniting in purpose.
Sometimes curved yet unyielding,
straight yet not arrogant.
Sometimes clashing without chaos,
parting yet not severed.
Now and then, forceful and impassioned,
or resentful and hesitant.
Suddenly floating lightly and swiftly,
then pausing, lingering, and branching out.
Sometimes dense and hurried,
repeating and clustering tightly;
crisscrossing continuously,
fleeing and pressing urgently.
Applause and repeated praise,
without a moment's pause.
Magnificent, exquisite, strangely grand,
beyond full comprehension.
As for its leisurely elegance,
both grand and delicate in due measure.
Clear and harmonious, smooth and flowing,
undulating and variegated.
Serenely gentle and joyful,
gracefully顺从 and winding.
Sometimes venturing into peril, seizing the moment,
darting through gaps, approaching danger.
Like the cry of a lone kūn bird in a clear pond,
or wings of a floating swan soaring over layered cliffs.
Intricate patterns and splendid tails,
fluttering and streaming apart.
Faint breezes and lingering echoes,
soft and graceful, swaying gently.
Sometimes plucking and brushing swiftly,
ethereal and shimmering, cool and sharp.
Lightly moving, floating strokes,
bright, skillful, and wise.
Swift but not rushed,
lingering but not stagnant.
Fluttering and drifting afar,
subtle tones swiftly fading.
Heard from a distance,
like luán and phoenixes harmonizing in play among the clouds;
observed up close,
like myriad blossoms blooming, shining in the spring breeze.
Rich and varied in postures,
excellent in beginning and commendable in end.
Alas, so exquisite and magnificent,
how endless its transformations!
As in early spring,
adorned in timely splendor,
one takes friends along,
to wander and play.
Crossing orchid gardens,
ascending layered heights;
leaving behind deep woods,
shaded by splendid flora;
facing clear streams,
composing new poems.
Praising the ease of fish and dragons,
delighting in the bloom of all plants.
Tuning the legacy melodies of Chónghuà,
sighing with longing and deep thought.
Or in ornate halls, intimate feasts,
with close friends and dear guests,
savory dishes served aplenty,
fine wine clear and mellow.
Presenting "Nán Jīng,"
striking up "Xī Qín,"
continuing "Líng Yáng,"
passing through "Bā Rén."
Varied uses mingled and arose together,
captivating all listeners, astounding the spirit.
Considering their unique merits and comparing their artistry,
how could shēng and yuè instruments ever match?
If ranking the suitable melodies,
then "Guǎng Líng Zhǐ Xī,"
"Dōng Wǔ Tài Shān;"
"Fēi Lóng Lù Míng,"
"Kūn Jī Yóu Xián."
Alternating in performance,
sounding as if natural.
Flowing and graceful, delicate and charming,
calming restlessness, washing away worries.
Extending to folk ballads,
the five tunes of Cài shì.
"Wáng Zhāo," "Chǔ Fēi,"
"Qiān Lǐ Bié Hè."
There are also occasional pieces,
filling in gaps when needed,
that are worth observing too.
Yet, unless one is broad-minded and far-reaching,
they cannot roam and play with it.
Unless one is deep and serene,
they cannot linger idly with it.
Unless one is unrestrained and open,
they cannot be without restraint with it.
Unless one is of the utmost refinement,
they cannot analyze its principles with it.
If discussing its form and momentum,
detailing its tonal character;
the instrument harmonious, thus the resonance transcendent,
strings taut, thus the sound clear;
spacing distant, thus the tone subdued,
strings long, thus the frets resonate.
Its nature pure and serene, with upright principle,
embodying the ultimate virtue of peace.
Truly, it can stir the heart and will,
and release deep emotions.
Therefore, those with sorrow hearing it,
none are not grieved and distressed,
saddened and heartbroken.
Harboring grief and sighs,
unable to restrain themselves.
Those in health and joy hearing it,
then delight and happiness release,
dancing and leaping with joy.
Lingering in boundless delight,
laughing heartily all day.
If the peaceful listen to it,
then it nurtures joy and pleasure,
serene and profound in true essence.
Tranquil and content with antiquity,
abandoning affairs, forgetting the self.
Thus, Bó Yí through it became廉洁,
Yán Huí through it became benevolent,
Bǐ Gàn through it became loyal,
Wěi Shēng through it became faithful,
Huì Shī through it became eloquent,
Wàn Shí through it became cautious in speech.
Others extending from these examples,
the outcomes are not uniform;
same destination, different paths,
some ornate, some plain.
Gathering central harmony to unite all things,
all daily used without loss.
Its power to move people and stir things,
is indeed vast.
At this moment,
the sounds of bells and stones fall silent,
wind and string instruments hold their breath.
Wáng Bào ceases his songs,
Dí Yá loses his taste.
Tiān Wú leaps joyfully in the deep abyss,
Wáng Qiáo descends through parting clouds.
The yuèzhuó phoenix dances in the courtyard,
roaming maidens float gracefully to gather.
Moved by heaven and earth to achieve harmony,
how much more the myriad creeping creatures.
Praising this instrument's sublime excellence,
I chant these verses to console myself.
Forever shall I use it without weariness,
truly valued through all ages.
Epilogue:
Serene is the virtue of the qin,
unfathomable indeed;
pure in form and far-reaching in spirit,
vast beyond reaching.
Fine material and skilled hands,
encountered in this present age;
rich harmonies and blended tones,
crowning all arts.
Few are those who understand music,
who can truly cherish it?
To fully comprehend the elegant qin,

A Letter Breaking Off Friendship with Shān Jùyuán
Kāng writes:
You once spoke of me to Yǐngchuān,
and I have always considered your words insightful.
Yet I often wonder at this intention,
since you are not yet thoroughly familiar with me—
how could you have formed such an understanding?
Two years ago, upon returning from Hédōng,
Xiǎnzōng and Ādū mentioned that you proposed I take your place,
though the matter did not materialize,
it revealed that you indeed do not know me.
You are versatile and accommodating,
tolerant of much and seldom critical.
I, however, am straightforward and narrow-minded,
with many things I cannot endure,
and it is by chance that we became acquainted.
Recently, hearing of your promotion,
I felt apprehensive and displeased.
Fearing you might be ashamed of being the only butcher,
and drag the sacrificial priest to assist you;
handing me the ceremonial knife,
to stain me with the smell of blood.
Thus, I shall fully explain to you what is feasible or not.
In my past readings,
I learned of those who are both principled and adaptable;
some say such people do not exist,
but now I believe they truly do.
There are inherent traits one cannot bear,
truly they cannot be forced.
Now, empty talk claims there are enlightened ones who endure all,
outwardly no different from the vulgar,
yet inwardly not losing their integrity;
flowing with the currents of the world,
without regret or stinginess arising.
Lǎozi and Zhuāng Zhōu,
are my teachers,
who personally held lowly positions.
Liǔxiàhuì and Dōngfāng Shuò,
were enlightened men,
content in humble stations.
How dare I belittle them?
Moreover, Zhòngní practiced universal love,
unashamed to hold the whip,
while Zǐwén had no desire for ministerial rank,
yet thrice ascended to be Lìngyǐn;
this shows the gentleman's intent to benefit all.
As it is said, the enlightened both universalize goodness without wavering,
and in hardship find contentment without distress.
From this perspective,
thus Yáo and Shùn ruling the world,
Xǔyóu dwelling in the cliffs,
Zǐfáng assisting Hàn,
Jiēyú singing as he walked,
their principles are one.
Looking up to these several gentlemen,
they can be said to have fulfilled their aspirations.
Thus, the gentleman's hundred actions,
take different paths but reach the same end.
They act according to their nature,
each adhering to what suits them.
Hence, there is the saying, "Some serve in court without leaving,
others enter the mountains without returning."
Moreover, Yánlíng admired Zǐzāng's ethos,
while Zhǎngqīng emulated Xiàngrú's integrity.
Where one's will and spirit are entrusted,
cannot be taken away.
Whenever I read the biographies of Shàngzǐpíng and Tàixiàowēi,
I am moved with admiration,
envisioning their character.
In youth, orphaned and exposed,
spoiled by mother and elder brother,
I did not delve into classical studies.
My nature is further lax and indolent,
with sluggish sinews and lax flesh.
My head and face often go unwashed for fifteen days a month.
Unless greatly uncomfortable or itchy,
I do not bathe.
Often, I hold back urination and resist rising,
only getting up when my bladder feels full.
Moreover, having indulged in freedom for long,
my disposition is proud and scattered,
simplicity conflicting with ritual,
laziness paired with negligence.
Yet I am tolerated by my peers,
who do not criticize my faults.
Further, reading Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozi,
only increases my unrestraint,
thus causing my desire for glory and advancement to wane daily,
while my inclination to follow my true self grows stronger.
This is like a young deer, if raised in captivity,
may submit to training;
but if restrained when grown,
it will frantically struggle against the reins,
even rushing into boiling water or fire.
Though adorned with golden bridles,
fed with fine delicacies,
it yearns more for the deep forests,
and longs for the lush grasslands.
Ruǎn Sìzōng never spoke of others' faults,
I often take him as my model,
yet cannot match him.
His innate nature surpassed others,
harmless to all things,
only exceeding in drinking.
Thus, he was constrained by the ritual-bound scholars,
hated like an enemy,
fortunately relying on the Great General's protection.
I am not as virtuous as Sìzōng,
and have flaws of arrogance and slackness.
Moreover, I do not understand human sentiments,
am blind to expediency,
lack the caution of Wànshí,
and am burdened by a tendency to speak too frankly.
Long engaged with affairs,
faults and conflicts arise daily.
Even if I wish to avoid trouble,
how could it be possible?
Furthermore, human relations have rituals,
the court has laws;
having deeply reflected on myself,
there are seven things I certainly cannot endure,
and two that are especially unacceptable.
I enjoy sleeping late,
yet the gatekeeper would incessantly call me;
first unendurable.
Carrying a qín, strolling and chanting,
hunting and fishing in the wilderness,
but with clerks and guards watching over me,
I cannot act freely;
second unendurable.
Sitting upright for hours,
numb and unable to move,
my body often full of lice,
scratching incessantly;
yet having to wrap in official robes,
bowing to superiors;
third unendurable.
I have never been adept at writing letters,
nor do I enjoy it;
yet in human affairs, there are many matters,
piling up on the desk.
Not responding to them,
violates teachings and damages duty;
if I force myself,
it cannot last.
Fourth unendurable.
I do not like mourning visits,
yet human custom holds them important.
I have been resented by those who do not forgive me,
to the point of being slandered.
Though I startle and blame myself,
my nature cannot be changed.
If I suppress my heart to conform to custom,
it would be hypocritical and insincere,
and ultimately I would not escape blame.
Without reputation as such;
fifth unendurable.
I dislike vulgar people,
yet must work alongside them.
Sometimes guests fill the seats,
their noise grating on the ears.
In the clamor and dust, a stinking place,
with a thousand changes and a hundred tricks,
all before one's eyes.
Sixth unendurable.
My heart is impatient,
yet official duties are overwhelming.
Administrative affairs burden my mind,
worldly matters complicate my thoughts.
Seventh unendurable.
Moreover, I often criticize Tāng and Wǔ,
and belittle Zhōu Gōng and Confucius;
in the human world, this does not stop at these matters,
and will inevitably be intolerable to the worldly teachings;
this is the first especially unacceptable.
With a stern heart that hates evil,
I lightly and recklessly speak directly,
erupting upon encountering issues;
this is the second especially unacceptable.
With a constricted, petty nature,
and统领 these nine afflictions,
even without external troubles,
there would be internal illness—
how could I long remain in the human world?
Also, I have heard Daoist teachings,
that taking shū and huángjīng,
can prolong life.
I firmly believe this.
Roaming mountains and marshes,
observing fish and birds,
brings great joy to my heart,
but once I take office,
these activities cease.
How can I abandon what I love,
to follow what I fear?
In mutual understanding between people,
the key is to recognize each other's innate nature,
and thereby support it.
Yǔ did not force Bóchéngzǐ,
to preserve his integrity;
Zhòngní did not borrow an umbrella from Zǐxià,
To protect their shortcomings.
In the past, Zhūgě Kǒngmíng did not force Xú Shù to enter Shǔ,
and Huà Zǐyú did not compel Guǎn Níng to accept high office.
This can be said to be capable of maintaining relationships from start to finish,
truly understanding one another.
You see that straight wood cannot be made into wheels,
and crooked wood cannot be used as rafters;
it is because one does not wish to distort their innate talent,
but to let it find its proper place.
Thus, the four classes of people each have their occupations,
and each finds joy in fulfilling their aspirations.
Only the enlightened can comprehend this,
and this is within your understanding.
You should not, seeing your own fondness for ceremonial caps,
force the Yuè people to wear ornate headdresses.
Nor should you, loving putrid things yourself,
feed a young phoenix with dead rats.
I have recently been studying the art of nurturing life,
rejecting external glory and splendor,
abandoning rich flavors,
letting my mind wander in solitude,
valuing inaction above all.
Even without the nine troubles,
I would still not care for what you favor,
and moreover, I suffer from a heart ailment,
which has recently grown increasingly severe.
In my private reflections, I have tested myself,
and found I cannot endure what I do not enjoy.
I have examined myself thoroughly.
If the path ends and the road runs out,
then so be it.
There is no need for you to wrong me unjustly,
driving me to a desperate plight.
I have recently lost the joy of my mother and brother,
and my heart is often filled with sorrow.
My daughter is thirteen,
my son is eight,
not yet adults;
and moreover, they are often ill.
Reflecting on this fills me with anguish,
how can I put it into words?
Now I only wish to remain in my humble lane,
teaching and nurturing my children and grandchildren,
occasionally sharing stories with relatives and old friends,
recounting the experiences of a lifetime.
A cup of unrefined wine,
a tune played on the zither,
and my aspirations are fully met.
If you persist in harassing me without cease,
it is merely to recruit me for official service,
to benefit the needs of the times.
You have long known that I am careless and unrefined,
unfit for practical affairs,

If it is said that while ordinary people all crave glory,

this is the closest to the truth that can be expressed.
However, for one with great talent and broad-mindedness,

that is truly commendable.
As for me, plagued by many illnesses,

this is where I truly fall short.

If you are eager for us to tread the path of royalty together,
hoping to bring me to it,
expecting mutual joy and benefit,

Unless there is deep enmity between us,
you would not go to such lengths.
There was a rustic who found joy in warming his back in the sun and thought celery delicious,

My thoughts are as stated,
both to clarify matters for you,

A Letter Severing Ties with Lǚ Chángtì
Kāng writes:
In the past, our ages were close,
and so we met often and grew close.
You were sincere in your intentions,
leading to a strong friendship.
I thus considered you a closest friend.
Though our paths in life differed,
our affection never waned.
Later, I came to know Ādū slightly,
and found him determined and insightful.
I often rejoiced that your family had such a younger brother.
However, last year, Ādū confided in me,
expressing genuine anger at your intentions to expose him.
I strongly discouraged him,
trusting that you would not press the matter,
so he followed my advice.
I then informed you,
and because he complied with me,
you reconciled with him,
all out of concern for your family's reputation,
hoping to keep both sides unharmed.
Moreover, you promised me you would never attack Dū,
swearing on the bond between father and son.
I was deeply moved by your solemn words,
comforted and reassured Dū,
and he thus set his mind at ease.
Yet, without renewing any intent toward you,
you secretly harbored doubts,
covertly submitted accusations against Dū,
and were the first to falsely confess and implicate him.
For Dū's sake,
I trusted you and said nothing more.
How could I have imagined you concealed such malicious intent?
Dū's endurance of you
was entirely due to my words.
Now that Dū has been condemned,
I am the one who has failed him.
My failure toward Dū
stems from your betrayal of me.
Disheartened and at a loss,
what more is there to say!
In light of this,
I have no desire to maintain our friendship any longer.
The noblemen of old, when severing ties, did not resort to ugly words.
From now on, we part ways!
At this farewell, I am filled with regret.

A Collection of Divination Doubts
There was a Master Hóngdá:
broad and expansive in his bearing,
serene and unconstrained,
upright yet unbridled,
incorruptible yet not cutting.
Transcending his age and standing alone,
he cherished jade within while clothed in coarse cloth.
In friendship, he did not lightly agree;
in office, he did not seek advancement.
He always believed that loyalty, trustworthiness, sincerity, and respect,
practiced with straightforwardness,
could enable one to dwell among the nine barbarian tribes,
travel through the eight wild lands,
float upon the vast sea,
and tread the source of the Yellow River.
Armor and weapons were not to be feared,
nor fierce beasts a cause for worry.
Thus, he harbored no cunning intentions,
remaining pure and simple in tranquility;
composed and unrestrained,
he forgot all likes and dislikes.
He regarded the Way of Heaven as a single principle,
unconcerned with the trivial details of things.
Yet, as the Great Way had long been obscured,
cunning and artifice flourished;
the world was entangled and complicated,
and human emotions were endlessly varied.
Where profit lay,
people flocked like birds chasing a phoenix.
Wealth accumulated corruption,
high status gathered resentment;
the active were often burdened,
the tranquil seldom troubled.
Thus, he thought of the recluses in the hills,
and took pleasure in angling by the streams.
Thereupon, he pondered deeply,
transcending and losing himself.
Since the man of Yǐng is gone,
who will be my touchstone?
I cannot see the sages,
but hope to hear from divination.
So he went to the cottage of Grand Historian Zhèngfù,
and inquired, saying:
"I have doubts,
and wish for you to divine them."
Zhèngfù then sat upright, holding the yarrow stalks,
wiped the table, and set out the tortoise shell, saying:
"What is your question?"
The master said:
"Should I strive to express my sincerity,
speak forthrightly in the imperial court,
and not yield to princes and dukes?
Or should I be humble and compliant,
following orders and bending with the wind,
giving mere surface assent?
Should I be kind and broadly nurturing,
giving without claiming virtue?
Or should I pursue worldly gains,
seeking only to fit in and please?
Should I live in seclusion, practicing righteousness,
and uphold utmost sincerity? Or should I embellish and deceive,
cultivating empty fame?
Should I expel the wicked and flatterers,
hold fast to integrity without wavering,
and clarify right and wrong?
Or should I be arrogant and glib,
wielding cunning and employing stratagems,
acting as a schemer?
Should I join Wáng Qiáo and Chìsōng as companions?
Or advance like Yī Zhì,
and befriend Shàngfǔ?
Should I hide my scales and conceal my brilliance,
like a dragon in the deep?
Or should I spread my wings and lift my voice,
like a swan among the clouds?
Should I outwardly adapt my form,
inwardly conceal my feelings,
bend with the times,
sink unnoticed into obscurity;
though in the human world,
truly dwell in darkness?
Or should I be fervent in purity,
sharp in thought and essence,
acting differently from the world,
yet mind aligned with customs;
ever striving to be heard, always bustling?
Should I be detached and unrestrained,
without pride or ambition;
uniting self and other as one,
neither contending nor yielding;
letting my mind wander in purity,
suddenly sitting in forgetfulness;
chasing Fúxī and Shénnóng yet falling short,
feeling sorrow on the midway path?
Or should I be impassioned for grandeur,
stirred by noble sentiments;
confronting the emperor above,
overawing generals and ministers below;
dignified in countenance,
proudly holding myself aloft;
often as if deprived of my post,
nursing resentment and discontent?
Should I amass wealth in billions,
dine with chimes and tripods;
recline amid fragrances,
and lovely beauties?
Or should I toil with my body and strength,
clearing away thorns;
dwelling in mountains, drinking from valleys,
resting against cliffs?
Should I be like Bófèn and Zhòngkān,
paired as the two eights;
repelling Gòng and Gǔn,
causing them to lose their place?
Or like the man of Jīshān,
the father of Yǐngshuǐ;
disdaining Tángyú,
and laughing at Dàyǔ?
Should I be like Tàibó, concealing virtue,
yielding in obscurity without acclaim?
Or like Jì Zhá, displaying integrity and righteousness,
admiring Zǐzāng?
Should I be like Lǎodān, pure, subtle, and mysterious,
guarding the profound and embracing the One?
Or like Zhuāng Zhōu, equating things and embracing change,
penetrating and unrestrained?
Should I be like Yíwú, unbound and free,
yet ultimately achieving hegemony?
Or like Lǔ Lián, despising the world and following his will,
speaking loftily and calmly?
Should I be like Shìnánzǐ, divinely brave and inwardly firm,
with aspirations deep as mountains and abysses?
Or like Máo Gōng and Lìn Shēng, dragon-striding and tiger-pacing,
admiring the brave?
Which path brings gain, which loss?
What is ominous, what auspicious?
Times change, customs shift;
people value and crave fame.
Zāng Wén did not yield his position to Liǔ Xiàhuì,
Gōngsūn did not attribute merit to Dǒng Shēng;
Jiǎ Yì once served a wise ruler,
yet Jiàng Guàn showed anger and raised voices.
Now, a thousand dragons race together,
ten thousand steeds gallop in campaign;
chaotically competing,
passing like shooting stars.
How dare I not seek counsel from the experienced!"
Grand Historian Zhèngfù said:
"I have heard that the perfect person does not read faces,
the enlightened does not divine.
As for you, sir,
culture and brightness reside within,
you appear plain and embrace simplicity.
Inwardly, your heart is without shame;
outwardly, you do not betray customs.
In friendship, you do not seek profit;
in office, you do not scheme for emolument.
You reflect on past and present,
cleansing emotions and desires.
Being thus,
you may swim at Lǚliáng,
and bathe at Tānggǔ;
you are about to behold the great roc in the southern sea,
so why worry about the twists and turns of the human world!"
One Essay on Nourishing Life
Some in the world claim that immortality can be attained through learning,
and eternal life achieved by effort.
Others say the maximum lifespan is one hundred twenty years,
identical across ancient and modern times;
beyond this limit,
all claims are but deceptive falsehoods.
Both views miss the truth.
Allow me to briefly discuss this.
Though immortals have not been seen with our own eyes,
records in texts,
and accounts in historical chronicles,
when compared and examined,
confirm their certain existence.
They seem to have received unique endowments,
bestowed by nature,
not achievable through accumulated learning.
As for attaining longevity through proper guidance and nurturing,
to fulfill one's natural lifespan,
the upper limit can exceed a thousand years,
the lower limit several hundred years—
this is indeed possible.
Yet people in general lack mastery in this,
hence none can achieve it.
How can this be explained?
Take consuming medicine to induce sweating—
sometimes it fails;
yet when shame arises,
sweat pours forth profusely.
Fasting a whole morning
brings ravenous thoughts of food,
but Zēngzǐ, immersed in grief, fasted seven days without hunger.
Sitting late at night
brings drowsiness and sleepiness;
yet harboring deep sorrow
keeps one awake until dawn.
A stiff brush combs the hair,
strong wine reddens the face—
these barely achieve their effects;
but a warrior's rage
strikingly alters his appearance,
making hair stand and lift his cap.
From this it follows that
the spirit's relation to the body
is like a ruler to the state.
When the spirit is agitated within,
the body deteriorates without;
just as when the ruler is foolish above,
the state falls into chaos below.
Farming in the era of Tāng,
if a field received even one irrigation,
though it ultimately withered,
the irrigated one would perish last;
thus the benefit of one watering
cannot be denied.
Yet people often say one anger cannot harm one's nature,
one grief cannot injure the body;
taking them lightly and indulging freely
is like ignoring the gain of one irrigation
yet expecting fine grain from parched sprouts.
Therefore, the noble person knows the body relies on the spirit to stand,
and the spirit depends on the body to exist.
Realizing life's principle is easily lost,
they understand a single fault can harm vitality.
Thus they cultivate nature to preserve spirit,
calm the mind to protect the body.
Love and hate do not dwell in emotions,
worry and joy do not linger in thoughts.
Serene and unaffected,
the body's energy remains harmonious;
further, through breathing exercises,
and consuming nourishment to sustain health;
they unite body and spirit,
aiding both inner and outer aspects.
As for broadcast sowing,
ten hú per mǔ
is called good farmland—
this is the common standard.
Yet people don't know intensive planting
can yield over a hundred hú.
The field and seeds are the same,
but differing cultivation methods
lead to vastly different harvests.
To say merchants lack tenfold profits,
farmers have no hope for hundred-hú yields,
is to cling to convention without change.
Moreover, beans make one heavy,
elms induce sleep,
héhuān alleviates anger,
xuāncǎo dispels sorrow—
known to both wise and foolish.
Pungent foods harm eyes,
pork and fish aren't nourishing—
common knowledge in the world.
Lice on the head turn black,
musk deer eating cypress become fragrant,
necks in rugged lands grow goiters,
teeth in Jìn turn yellow.
Extending this reasoning,
all ingested energies steam into nature and dye the body,
none fail to correspond.
How could steaming only make heavy, not light;
harming only dim, not brighten;
fumigating only yellow, not harden;
perfuming only fragrant, not prolong?
Thus Shénnóng said:
Superior medicine nurtures life,
medium medicine nurtures nature—
truly understanding the principles of life and nature,
one supports them to achieve harmony.
Yet people fail to observe this,
seeing only the five grains,
indulging in music and beauty;
eyes dazzled by colors,
ears filled with decadent sounds;
flavors sear their organs,
alcohol boils their intestines,
fragrances decay their marrow.
Joy and anger disrupt their vital energy,
thoughts consume their spirit,
sorrow and joy damage their calm essence.
With such a tiny body,
assailed from multiple fronts;
an easily depleted form,
attacked from within and without;
the body is not wood or stone—
how can it last long?
Those most reckless
eat and drink without restraint,
breeding countless illnesses.
Tireless in lust,
they exhaust themselves utterly.
Harmed by wind and cold,
injured by various poisons,
they die prematurely amid numerous troubles.
The world laughs and mourns them,
calling them poor at preserving life.
As for those who err in self-care,
losing it in subtle ways,
accumulating slight into damage,
damage into decline,
graying from decline,
aging from gray hair,
ending from old age—
bewildered as if without cause.
Those of average wisdom or less
call it natural.
Even if slightly aware, they sigh,
regretting the start of their plight,
yet fail to guard against dangers before signs appear.
This is like Duke Huán clinging to fatal illness
and raging at Biǎn Què's foresight;
taking the day pain is felt
as the beginning of sickness.
Harm forms in subtlety,
but rescue comes at manifestation—
hence futile treatments arise.
Roaming in the realm of ordinary folk,
thus they have only commonplace lifespans.
Looking up and observing down,
all is thus.
Using the majority as proof,
finding comfort in similarity,
they claim the principles of heaven and earth
end here.
Even hearing of life cultivation,
they judge by their limited view,
deeming it untrue.
Next, some with little doubt
still hardly know the way.
Others strive to take medicine
for half or a full year,
toiling without effect;
their will wanes with fatigue,
abandoning the path midway.
Some add a trickle of gain
while losing a flood through leaks;
yet expect sitting to bring clear reward.
Others suppress desires,
forsaking glory and aspirations,
while temptations remain before their eyes,
hopes set decades ahead.
Fearing loss on both sides,
hesitation within,
inner battles raging,
external lures beckoning,
near and far conflicting—
thus they fail again.
The profoundest truths are subtle,
knowable through reason,
hard to recognize by sight.
Like the yùzhāng tree,
it takes seven years to perceive its growth;
yet with restless, competitive hearts,
they tread the path of rare tranquility;
intentions swift but progress slow,
hopes near but response far.
Thus none can carry it through to the end.
Those who are casual, having seen no results, do not seek it;
Those who seek it lose their progress due to lack of focus;
Those who rely on one-sided methods achieve nothing for lack of comprehensiveness;
Those who chase techniques drown themselves in trivial arts.
All cases like these
show that among those who desire it,
not one in ten thousand can succeed.
Those skilled in nurturing life,
however, are not like this.
They are clear, empty, tranquil, and peaceful,
with few selfish desires.
Knowing that fame and status harm virtue,
they disregard them and do not pursue;
it is not a case of desiring but forcibly restraining.
Recognizing that rich flavors injure one's nature,
they abandon them without a second thought;
it is not a case of coveting and then suppressing.
External things that burden the mind are not retained;
the spirit and energy become pure and luminous, standing alone.
Vast and free from worries,
serene and without anxious thoughts.
Further, they preserve it with unity,
and nurture it with harmony.
Harmony and principle daily assist each other,
merging with the great flow of nature.
Then they steam themselves with língzhī,
moisten with sweet springs,
bask in the morning sun,
and soothe with the five-stringed lute.
Acting through non-action, they attain naturally,
their bodies subtle, minds profound.
Forgetting joy, then happiness is full;
letting go of life, then the body endures.
Proceeding in this way,
one may nearly compare in longevity to Xiànmén,
and contend in years with Wángqiáo.
How can it be said that such a thing does not exist?
A Response to the Difficulty in the Discourse on Nurturing Life
The response states:
The reason for valuing wisdom and esteeming action
lies in their ability to enhance life and enrich the self.
However, when desires stir, regrets arise;
when wisdom is applied, preconceptions form.
Once preconceptions form, ambitions unfold and material pursuits follow;
once regrets arise, troubles accumulate and the self is endangered.
If these two are not kept within but instead engage with the external,
they only bring disaster to the self,
and do not serve to enrich life.
Though desires originate from humans,
they are not aligned with the true path of morality.
Just as a tree may host borers,
which, though born from the tree,
are not beneficial to it.
Thus, when borers thrive, the tree decays;
when desires prevail, the self withers.
Hence, desires and life cannot coexist,
fame and the self cannot both endure—
this is roughly clear.
Yet the world fails to realize this,
mistaking the indulgence of desires for the preservation of life.
Though they have the intention to enrich life,
they do not understand the principle of nurturing life.
Thus, they act in ways that lead to death.
Therefore, the ancients,
knowing that wine and lust are sweet poison,
discarded them as if casting away refuse;
recognizing fame and status as fragrant bait,
they turned away without a glance.
They ensured that actions sufficed to support life,
without excess toward material things,
knowing to rectify themselves,
without striving for external gains.
They turned away from what harms
and moved toward what benefits,
this is the way to use wisdom for fulfilling life.
Thus, the beauty of wisdom
lies in its enhancement of life,
not in envying life as something precious.
It values joy and harmony without entanglement,
how can one hasten after wisdom and belittle the self,
or labor under desires and devalue life?
Moreover, when sages treasure their positions
and regard wealth and honor as lofty,
it is generally said that a ruler is honored as the Son of Heaven,
possessing the wealth of the four seas.
The people cannot exist without a sovereign,
and the sovereign cannot stand without respect.
Thus, the ruler's position is honored for the sake of all under heaven,
not for the sake of one individual's wealth and honor.
It is also said:
Wealth and honor are what people desire,
likely because in decadent times, people despise poverty and lowliness
and crave wealth and honor.
Unable to transcend glory and live content in poverty,
they are restrained to follow the proper path.
If they cannot be made to strive without contention,
their hearts are allowed to compete.
Since the mean cannot be attained,
they are given to recklessness or stubbornness.
This is but common talk,
not implying that the perfected person should covet wealth and honor.
The sage rules the world out of necessity,
with a heart for all things,
nurturing the masses,
guiding the self by the Way,
and sharing self-contentment with all under heaven.
Serenely, they take non-action as their task;
openly, they regard the world as public.
Though occupying the ruler's position,
enjoying the homage of myriad states,
they are as calm as a common scholar receiving guests.
Though they raise the dragon banner
and wear ornate robes,
they are as unassuming as if clad in plain cloth.
Thus, ruler and ministers forget their status above,
while the people have ample households below.
How could they urge the people to honor themselves,
carve up the world for personal gain,
regard wealth and honor as lofty,
and endlessly desire them in their hearts?
Moreover, when Zǐwén was promoted three times,
his expression showed no added joy;
when Liǔ Huì was dismissed three times,
his countenance showed no added sorrow.
Why?
The honor of being prime minister
is not as precious as virtue and righteousness;
the disgrace of three dismissals
does not harm the beauty of purity and essence.
These two men experienced wealth and honor in their lives,
yet never let official ranks burden their hearts,
thus regarding glory and disgrace as one.
From this perspective,
how can one speak of a desire for wealth and honor?
I ask: why must one,
when fine garments are not displayed in a dark room,
heed the crowd
and let joy or sorrow be moved by praise or slander?
Thus,
the trouble with desire is in its attainment;
upon attainment, one fears its loss.
If one fears loss, there is nothing one will not do.
How can those in high position avoid arrogance?
How can those holding fullness avoid overflow?
How can their pursuits avoid being unscrupulous?
How can their gains avoid being lost?
Moreover, when a noble person speaks,
goodness is responded to from a thousand miles away—
how does this depend on many desires and valuing gain?
By upholding laws and following principles,
not entangled in worldly nets,
they respect themselves through blamelessness,
and find ease in not holding office.
Their hearts wander in the Way and righteousness,
they rest content in humble dwellings.
Tranquil and joyful without conflict,
their spirit and energy flow smoothly.
How can they need glory and splendor
to then be considered noble?
They plow for food,
raise silkworms for clothing;
with food and clothing covering their needs,
they have surplus wealth from the world.
Like a thirsty person drinking from a river,
content and satisfied,
they do not envy great floods.
How can they need to amass wealth
to then be considered rich?
This is how a noble person applies their heart.
They regard fame and status as superfluous growths,
and material resources as dust and grime.
What use have they for wealth and honor?
Thus, what is difficult to attain in the world
is not wealth,
nor glory,
but the affliction of insufficient contentment!
Those who are content,
even farming side by side in the fields,
clad in coarse cloth and eating simple food,
are they not self-content?
Those who are discontent, even if provided with the whole world
and entrusted with all things,
still remain unsatisfied.
Thus, the content need nothing external,
while the discontent need everything external.
Needing everything,
they find lack wherever they go;
needing nothing,
they find sufficiency wherever they are.
They do not indulge their ambitions with glory and splendor,
nor do they conform to vulgar trends in obscurity.
Blending with the myriad things in their course,
they cannot be swayed by honor or disgrace—
this is true wealth and honor.
Therefore, those who forsake nobility yet desire it
end up in lowliness;
those who forget wealth yet crave it
end up in poverty.
Such is the natural principle.
Now, to dwell in glory and splendor yet worry,
even growing old with them,
is to live a life of perpetual sorrow.
Thus, Lǎozǐ said:
There is no greater joy than having no worries,
no greater wealth than knowing contentment.
This expresses it.
An objection states:
To feel and think of home,
to hunger and seek food—
these are natural principles.
How true these words are!
Now, it is not about preventing one from having a home or food,
but about ensuring that home and food are obtained in accordance with reason.
To desire without forethought
is the stirring of innate nature;
to feel only after understanding
is the application of intellect.
When innate nature stirs,
it responds to things appropriately,
and is content without excess;
when intellect is applied,
it pursues based on feelings,
tiring endlessly without cease.
Thus, the worries of the world
and the origins of misfortune
often lie in the application of intellect,
not in the stirring of innate nature.
If a blind man encounters a home,
he would feel the same toward Xī Shī and Mó Mǔ;
if a deaf man forgets taste,
bran and chaff would be as sweet as fine grains.
How could they distinguish between worthy and foolish, beautiful and ugly,
letting love and hate disturb their hearts?
The noble person understands that intellect, being inconstant, harms life,
and desires, by chasing objects, injure innate nature.
Thus, when intellect is applied, it is restrained with tranquility;
when innate nature stirs, it is corrected with harmony,
so that intellect stops at tranquility,
and innate nature is satisfied with harmony.
Thereafter, the spirit becomes silently pure,
the body is perfected through harmony,
burdens are removed and harms eliminated,
and one is reborn with them.
This is what is called "not seeing what is desirable,
so the heart is not disturbed."
Even if flavors constantly stain the mouth,
and sounds and sights have already stirred the heart,
one can dismiss them with supreme reason,
and overcome them with ample calculation.
How can this be explained?
For instance, one desiring office does not covet the sovereign's position,
and one longing for home does not scheme against relatives.
Why?
Knowing what one cannot obtain,
one should not entertain such thoughts.
Thus, a wine lover restrains himself from poisoned ale,
and a glutton endures hunger rather than eat spoiled meat.
Understanding the principles of fortune and misfortune,
they turn away without confusion,
and abandon without doubt.
How could they resent not having indulged in heavy drinking or feasting before?
Moreover, the maidservant at the inn:
the ugly one values herself for her ugliness,
the beautiful one is demeaned for her beauty.
Though the forms of beauty and ugliness are visible to the eye,
their values differ,
because the truth of right and wrong is established first,
so beauty and ugliness cannot sway it.
If it is said that reason is sufficient within,
and one masters it to govern the external,
what thing can silently affect one?
From this perspective,
when innate energy is naturally harmonious,
there is no need for defensive barriers;
when emotions and will are naturally calm,
there is no stagnation or obstruction.
The many burdens of the world
arise from unclear perception.
Moreover, it is common human nature:
what is distant,
however great, is often neglected;
what is near,
however small, is often retained.
What is the reason?
Truly, it is because the immediate and the remote contend,
and perceptions differ based on circumstances.
During the three-year mourning period, refraining from intimacy
is a prohibition of ritual,
yet none violate it;
wine and women are enemies of the body,
yet none can abandon them.
From this,
ritual prohibitions, though minor, are not breached,
while bodily enemies, though remote, are not discarded.
Yet, if one could hold the map of the world in the left hand
while the right hand brings harm to oneself,
even a fool would not do it.
This shows that the world is lighter than one's own body,
and wine and women are lighter than the world,
which is further evident.
Yet people in the world sacrifice themselves for these,
dying without regret,
thus trading the important for the trivial—
is this not turning from the remote to the immediate?
The wise are not so.
They assess the weight before acting,
and measure gains and losses to preserve themselves;
understanding the principle of immediate and remote alike,
they prepare for the distant as if it were near,
and are cautious of the subtle as if it were obvious.
Alone, they walk the gate of all wonders,
thus remaining safe from start to end.
How different is this
from those who indulge desires for momentary pleasure?
An objection states:
Sages exhaust principle and fulfill nature,
so they should enjoy long lives,
yet Yáo and Confucius lived at most a hundred years,
or as few as seventy.
Could they have been negligent in guiding and nurturing life?
Consider that Yáo and Confucius, though endowed with limited fate,
practiced guidance and nurturing to live out their longevity.
This is the result of exhausting principle—
it is not that they failed to nurture life and still reached a hundred years.
Moreover, Confucius exhausted principle and fulfilled nature,
living to seventy,
while a rustic farmer, with six flaws and foolishness,
lived to a hundred and twenty.
If one took Confucius's utmost refinement
and endowed it with the farmer's utmost clumsiness,
then talk of a thousand years
would be no surprise.
Furthermore, among sages,
some diminish themselves for the world,
displaying conduct and revealing merits,
making the world admire them,
moving thrice to form a capital;
some eat meagerly and toil personally,
managing the four directions,
with hearts weary and bodies strained,
their steps losing rhythm;
some devise hidden strategies,
involving spears and shields,
wielding might and waging war,
contending for merit and gain.
Some cultivate themselves to expose others'污秽,
display wisdom to startle the foolish,
borrowing high renown for a lifetime,
setting standards for the world;
others teach diligently and guide kindly,
gathering three thousand disciples,
with mouths tired from discourse,
bodies fatigued from bowing,
forms as if saving a child,
gaze as if managing the world.
Their spirits race to the edges of gain and loss,
their hearts gallop on the paths of glory and shame,
in the blink of an eye,
they have already twice traversed beyond the cosmos.
Compare this to inward vision and reverse listening,
cherishing breath and conserving essence;
understanding clearly in all directions,
yet unholding and non-acting;
leaving the world to sit in forgetfulness,
preserving nature and perfecting truth—
I cannot equate them.
Now, it is not that pines and cypresses
are no different from elms and willows.
Yet pines and cypresses grow,
each fulfilling their nature through good soil.
If a pine is nurtured in ash soil,
it withers in middle age;
planted on a steep cliff,
it flourishes anew each day.
This is one perspective on nurturing form.
Dòu Gōng took no tonics or treatments,
yet reached a hundred and eighty.
Was it not by playing the zither to harmonize his heart?
This is one evidence of nurturing spirit.
Silkworms in heat live eighteen days,
in cold, over thirty days,
though their allotted time cannot be exceeded,
yet care can double their vitality.
The warm and plump die early,
the cool and lean deplete slowly—
this can clearly be recognized.
Stable horses, raised but not ridden,
all live to sixty years.
The fatigued decay quickly,
the whole-formed die hard—
this too is evident.
The wealthy and noble often suffer harm,
for many assail them;
rustics live long,
for few injure them.
This is also visible.
Now, if one can make the eyes function like the blind's,
the mouth taste like the deaf's,
avoiding tools that harm life,
and mastering things that benefit nature,
then one may begin to discuss nurturing life and nature.
The objection states:
Shénnóng initiated the practice of eating grains,
enabling birds and beasts to fly and roam,
and people to see and breathe.
Now, it is not claimed that the five grains were not initiated by Shénnóng;
since superior medicines are mentioned,
why also advocate for the five grains?
It is because superior medicines are rare and scarce,
difficult to obtain,
while the five grains are easy to cultivate,
agriculturally sustainable and enduring.
They serve to aid the common people and prevent premature death,
thus both are preserved.
The wise focus on the greater aspects,
while the unworthy dwell on the lesser.
This all originates from the same person,
and when dāngguī is used to relieve pain,
its application is continuous;
with plows and hoes tilling the land,
their use never ceases.
How can nurturing life
be disregarded and not discussed?
This is likely due to familiarity with prior habits,
and suspicion toward the unknown.
Moreover, on plains there are dates and chestnuts,
in ponds there are water caltrops and foxnuts,
though not superior medicines,
they still surpass the humble reverence of millet and sorghum.
How can one claim that the means for sight and breath
rely solely on the five grains?
It is also said:
"The millets are fragrant,"
and indeed attract the spirits.
Duckweeds and pondweeds,
cannot match sumptuous feasts;
stagnant puddles and road-side puddles,
are no match for fine wines.
When offered in ancestral temples,
they move the spirits to bestow blessings.
This shows that spirits enjoy virtue and sincerity,
not relying on sustenance for life.
Just as the nine regions report on their duties,
each presenting local products,
to demonstrate sincerity.
It is further said:
Food and grains enter the body,
their benefits last no more than ten days,
demonstrating the evidence for nurturing life.
This is what burdens the body.
Now, it is not that food and grains lack benefits for filling the body,
but that extending life is not comparable to superior medicines.
Allow me to use this as a rebuttal.
Knowing that wheat is better than beans,
and rice surpasses millet,
is recognized through their effects.
If in a land without rice or millet,
beans and wheat would be treasured as nourishment,
considered unsurpassable.
Thus, if people do not know that superior medicines are better than rice and millet,
it is like insisting that beans and wheat are superior to weeds,
and claiming that rice and millet do not exist in the world.
If one can rely on medicine to prolong life,
then the inferiority of rice and millet
becomes evident.
The noble person knows this,
