so they align with the principles of nature,
using wondrous substances to nurture the body.
Planting the profound root in the initial yang,
inhaling the morning mist to nourish the spirit.
If now one relies on spring wine for longevity,
we have not heard of Gāoyáng having elderly with yellow hair;
if considering satiety and pleasure as virtue,
we have not heard of those feasting lavishly living to a hundred years.
Moreover, Rǎnshēng suffered from illness,
Yánzǐ died young.
In plentiful years, there is more sickness;
in famine years, less disease.
Thus, the Dí people eating rice developed leprosy,
sores,
and with grains, their blood became浮;
horses fed millet become heavy-footed;
wild geese eating grains become sluggish.
From this perspective,
birds and beasts owe no gratitude to the five grains,
nor do people receive virtue from farmlands.
Yet humans exhaust themselves to cultivate them,
and kill one another competing for them;
to support parents and honor superiors,
they use only fine grains and rice;
in banquets and celebrations,
only delicacies and fine wine.
Unaware that these all turn into foul fluids in muscles and armpits,
easily decaying and rotting quickly.
Initially sweet and fragrant,
they enter the body and become putrid,
exhausting and demeaning the spirit,
polluting the six viscera.
Foul vapors steam,
spontaneously generating calamities and pests.
They lead to gluttony and excess,
attracting hundreds of diseases.
Those who taste them find their palate ruined,
those who consume them have shortened lives.
How can they compare to flowing springs and sweet dew,
jade stamens and floral essences?
Golden elixirs and stone fungi,
purple ganoderma and huángjīng.
All contain the essence of myriad spirits,
uniquely emerging and wondrously born.
Their pure fragrance hardly fades,
harmonious energy fills abundantly.
They cleanse the five organs,
opening and illuminating them clearly.
Those who sip them feel their bodies lighten.
Furthermore, they refine the skeleton and transform the energy,
staining the bones and softening the sinews.
Washing away filth and moistening impurities,
the will soars to the blue clouds.
Continuing thus,
what need is there for the nourishment of the five grains?
Moreover, the young of the mulberry moth
are carried by the eumenid wasp,
a change in nature.
Oranges crossing the river become trifoliate oranges,
changing with the soil,
an alteration in form.
If one absorbs the energy of what is eaten,
returning to essence and transforming nature,
how could it be impossible?
Thus, Chìfǔ refined cinnabar and turned his hair red,
Juānzǐ used techniques to prolong life greatly,
Wòquán ate pine nuts and gained square pupils,
Chìsōng employed crystal to ride the mist,
Wùguāng used chives to grow long ears,
Qiōngshū ingested stone marrow to preserve youth,
Fānghuí transformed with mica,
Chāngróng changed her appearance with wild strawberries.
Examples like these,
are too numerous to detail.
Who can claim the five grains are supreme,
and that superior medicines are without benefit?
Moreover, they criticize that for a thousand years,
no one has seen such things,
claiming there are no such people.
But if you ask those who speak of it,
how would they recognize a thousand-year-old person?
How to distinguish them?
If comparing by form,
they are no different from others;
if testing by age,
the morning mushroom cannot know the full moon,
the mayfly cannot recognize the divine turtle.
Thus, though a thousand-year-old may be in the marketplace or court,
they are certainly beyond the discernment of those with limited perspective.
Péngzǔ lived seven hundred years,
Ānqī a thousand years,
yet the narrow-minded say records are false.
Liú Gēn slept long without eating,
some say he merely endured hunger;
Zhòngdū was naked in winter yet warm,
wore fur in summer yet cool,
Huán Tán called it accidental tolerance to cold and heat;
Lǐ Shàojūn recognized Duke Huán's jade bowl,
so Ruǎn Shēng called it fortune-telling;
and knowing Yáo offered the empire to Xǔyóu,
Yáng Xióng deemed it grandiose fabrication.
All such cases,
elevate Zhōu and Confucius as the standard,
devoting themselves solely to sincerity;
lower desires serve as whips,
unable to cease even if they wished.
Rushing within worldly teachings,
vying for skill in matters of honor and disgrace,
they diminish themselves by following the majority,
thoughts confined to their station,
causing extraordinary events to vanish from sight,
profound principles to be cut off by conventional discourse;
to speak of understanding change and subtleties,
is unheard of among them.
Long vexed in solitude,
they call it joyless;
deeply regretting lack of delicacies,
they call it self-inflicted sorrow.
Considering wine and sensuality as sustenance,
they deem longevity pointless.
Thus, what you consider joy
must involve grand carriages and processions,
with lavish feasts spread before you.
To deem such fulfillment as natural heavenly principle
is to enslave the body to material things,
lose ambition to desires,
and in examining the truth of life's nature,
be burdened by your own arguments.
The thirsty see only water,
the drinker seeks only wine,
all know these stem from ailments.
Now, if following desires is seen as fulfilling nature,
then the thirsty and the drunkard are not ill,
Indulgence in excess is not a fault,
as even the followers of Jié and Zhí attained naturalness,
but this is not the essence of our discourse to elucidate the ultimate principle.
The ultimate principle is indeed subtle,
easily drowned in worldly affairs,
yet one may seek it within oneself and later awaken to it,
or discern it by examining external things.
From youth to adulthood,
preferences and aversions rise and fall,
with periods of vigor and decline.
What brings joy in childhood
may be abandoned in maturity;
what is initially despised
may later be valued.
When something pleases,
it is deemed unshakable;
when it repulses,
it is seen as irredeemable.
Yet, with a change in circumstances,
feelings shift from their initial state.
If desires can alter,
how can we be sure that what we now indulge in
will not become foul?
Or that what was once scorned
may not turn into something wondrous?
If a lowly servant suddenly rose to high office,
even gatekeepers
would disregard and forget him.
Thus, it is said,
all such attachments are merely confined to a narrow perspective—
how can they be immutable?
Moreover, when hungry and eating,
as one nears the desired satisfaction,
joy fills the heart;
but once satiated,
it is casually set aside,
sometimes even with disgust.
Hence, even glory, wealth, wine, and sensual pleasures have their time to be forsaken.
The python is treasured in Yuè lands,
yet in the Central Plains, it is met with aversion;
embroidered robes are esteemed in Huáxià,
but in naked tribes, they are obtained and discarded.
When deemed useless,
they are like the python to the Central Plains
or the embroidered robes to the naked tribes.
If one regards great harmony as the ultimate joy,
then glory and splendor are not worth a glance;
if tranquility and simplicity are the finest flavors,
then wine and sensual pleasures are not to be admired.
If one finds contentment within,
the pleasures of the mundane world
are but dung—
what is there to cling to?
Nowadays, those who speak fail to see the essence of ultimate joy,
willingly shortening their lives
to follow their desires.
This is like Lǐ Sī betraying Confucianism
to indulge a momentary craving;
or like Zhǔfù, in his fervor,
dreaming of savoring the five tripods' delicacies.
Moreover, lingering in a fish market, one grows accustomed to its stench and scorns orchids and angelica,
just as the sea bird faced with a grand feast felt prolonged sorrow,
or Lord Wén covered his ears upon hearing elegant music.
Thus, to treat glory and splendor as essentials for life
and claim that even saving myriad generations would not bring joy—
this stems from having no inner mastery,
relying on external things for happiness.
Though external riches abound,
sorrow is ever-present.
With inner mastery,
one finds joy within to appreciate the external;
even without bells and drums,
happiness is already complete.
Therefore, those who attain their aims
do not depend on high rank;
those with ultimate joy
are not driven by insatiable desires.
Gains and losses cannot burden them.
Furthermore, when parents are ill
and recover from distress,
worry and joy coexist.
From this, it is clear
that having no joy at all might be preferable.
Then, is the absence of pleasure not the ultimate joy?
Thus, by following heavenly harmony in naturalness,
taking the Dào and virtue as teachers and friends,
contemplating the transformations of yīn and yáng,
and attaining eternal longevity;
entrusting oneself to nature for sustenance,
merging with heaven and earth in imperishability—
who can truly enjoy this?
There are five difficulties in nurturing life:
failure to extinguish fame and profit—
this is the first difficulty.
Failure to eliminate joy and anger—
this is the second.
Failure to abandon music and beauty—
this is the third.
Failure to cease indulging in flavors—
this is the fourth.
And a restless,发散 spirit—
this is the fifth.
If these five persist,
even if one's heart yearns for agelessness,
recites profound teachings,
savors the essence of excellence,
and breathes the primal energy,
one cannot avoid straying from one's discipline
and cutting life short.
With these five absent from the heart,
trust and compliance grow daily,
and mysterious virtue becomes whole.
Without praying for happiness, fortune comes;
without seeking longevity, life extends.
This is the effect of the great principle of nurturing life.
Yet some may act beyond even Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Sǔn,
devoted to benevolence and righteousness,
moving with balance and harmony,
free from heavy burdens,
and claim that human principles are fully realized,
thus esteeming themselves.
But without calming joy and anger,
pacifying the spirit and energy,
and hoping to repel old age and extend life—
such a thing has never been heard.
Some uphold lofty aspirations, emulating antiquity,
not valuing fame or position,
and thus regard themselves above the hustlers.
Others employ wisdom to navigate the world,
avoiding calamity,
and so hold themselves in high esteem.
In terms of self-cultivation, they are no different from elderly villagers who have lived long.
Speaking of preserving life,
they are lacking.
Some withdraw from the world, aloof from the crowd,
with harmonious and pure will and energy,
yet without abstaining from grains or consuming herbs,
it does little to delay an early death.
If one stores divine provisions,
masters the six energies,
and can contain light to gaze inward,
concentrate the spirit to return to simplicity,
rest the mind on the cliff of profound darkness,
and embrace energy by the shore of the vast infinite—
then aging can be repelled,
and life extended.
All these methods, combined in practice,
are indispensable.
Like axles, wheels, and hubs,
none can be missing from a carriage.
Yet people often hold biased views,
each prone to their own flaws:
Shān Bào focused inwardly and neglected the external,
while Zhāng Yì rushed outwardly and lost balance.
Qí, by deceitfully seizing Jìxī, met defeat;
Qín, by over-preparing against the Róng and Dí, exhausted itself.
These are the disasters of imbalance.
Accumulating goodness and upholding trust—
this is often heard in the world;
being cautious in speech,
moderating in eating and drinking—
scholars know this.
Beyond this,
little is understood.
Let us, with prior awareness,
speak to those who will awaken in the future.
Discourse on Music Having No Grief or Joy
A guest from Qín inquired of the host from Dōngyě:
"I have heard from previous discourses:
The music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
while the music of a fallen state is sorrowful and pensive.
Now order and chaos reside in governance,
and musical sounds respond to them.
Thus feelings of sorrow and pensiveness
are expressed in metal and stone instruments;
the appearance of peace and joy
takes form in pipe and string instruments.
Moreover, when Confucius heard the Sháo music,
he recognized the virtue of Emperor Shùn;
when Jìzhá listened to string music,
he understood the customs of various states.
These are established facts
that former sages never doubted.
Now you alone maintain that sound has no sorrow or joy -
what is the reasoning behind this?
If you have enlightened explanations,
I beg now to hear your argument."
The host replied to him:
"This principle has long been obscured,
with none willing to rescue it.
Thus through successive ages,
names and realities have been confused.
Now, receiving your guidance,
I shall speak of one aspect.
Heaven and earth combine their virtues,
and all things value life.
Cold and heat alternate in succession,
and the five phases thereby form.
Thus patterns manifest as five colors,
and issue forth as five tones.
The production of musical sounds
is like scents existing between heaven and earth.
Their goodness or lack thereof,
even when encountering turbidity and disorder,
their substance remains as it is
and does not change.
How could love or hate alter their nature,
or sorrow or joy change their measure?
When the gōng and shāng notes are collected and arranged,
and musical sounds achieve harmony,
this is the ultimate desire of the human heart,
where emotions and desires concentrate.
The ancients knew emotions cannot be indulged,
desires cannot be extreme,
so according to their function,
they constantly regulated them,
ensuring sorrow did not reach injury,
joy did not reach excess.
Following affairs with names,
things possess their designations.
Weeping is called sorrow,
singing is called joy.
This is the general principle.
Yet when we speak of joy,
do we mean merely bells and drums?
When we speak of sorrow,
do we mean merely crying and weeping?
Based on this,
jade and silk are not the substance of ritual respect,
song and dance are not the essence of sorrow.
How to clarify this?
Different regions have different customs -
their singing and weeping differ;
if used interchangeably,
some may hear weeping and feel joy,
others may hear singing and feel sorrow.
Yet the feelings of sorrow and joy remain the same.
Now using the same feelings
to produce myriad different sounds -
is this not proof that musical sounds lack constancy?
Yet harmonious musical sounds
affect people most deeply.
The laborer sings of his work,
the joyful dancer performs his achievement.
When one harbors a grieving heart within,
then urgent sorrowful words are stirred.
Words arranged become poetry,
sounds arranged become music.
Mixed together they are chanted,
gathered together they are heard.
The heart is moved by harmonious sounds,
emotions are stirred by bitter words.
Before sighs and lamentations cease,
tears already flow in streams.
The sorrowful heart hides within,
meeting harmonious sounds then emerges;
harmonious sounds have no fixed image,
yet the sorrowful heart has its master.
When the mastered sorrowful heart
relies on imageless harmonious sounds,
what it perceives and understands
is solely sorrow.
How could it further know the myriad different blowings
that make it stop by itself?
The flow of customs
eventually forms governance.
Therefore the state historian clarifies the successes and failures of governance,
examines the rise and fall of state customs,
chants of emotions and nature,
to admonish his superiors.
Hence it is said:
The music of a fallen state is sorrowful and pensive.
Joy, anger, sorrow, pleasure,
love, hate, shame, fear -
all these eight
are how people connect with things and transmit feelings,
distinguished into categories,
and cannot overflow.
Flavors are designated sweet or bitter,
now if I consider A virtuous and love him in my heart,
consider B foolish and hate him in my emotion,
then love and hate should belong to me,
while virtue and foolishness should belong to them.
Can I, because I love, call someone a 'loving person',
or because I hate, call someone a 'hating person'?
Should what pleases me be called 'pleasing flavor',
what angers me be called 'angering flavor'?
From this perspective,
external and internal have different functions,
others and self have distinct names.
Musical sounds should properly take good and bad as their essence,
then they have no connection to sorrow or joy.
Sorrow and joy should properly emerge only after emotional stimulation,
then they have no tie to musical sounds.
With both name and reality removed,
this becomes completely evident.
Moreover, when Jìzǐ was in Lǔ,
he collected poems and observed rituals
to distinguish the Fēng and Yǎ.
Did he merely rely on sounds to judge good and bad?
Also, when Confucius heard the Sháo music,
he admired its consistency,
thus he sighed in admiration -
why must one understand Emperor Shùn's virtue through the music
before praising its beauty?
Now having roughly clarified one aspect,
one may already grasp more than half the truth."
The Qín guest objected:
"Though customs vary across the eight directions,
and songs and lamentations differ vastly,
the feelings of sorrow and joy
cannot but be revealed.
When the heart is stirred within,
sound emerges from the heart.
Even if conveyed through other tones,
or expressed through additional sounds,
those skilled in listening and discernment
will naturally perceive it without allowing it to pass unnoticed.
In the past, when Bóyá played the qín,
Zhōng Zǐ knew his aspirations;
when a servant struck the qìng,
Zǐchǎn recognized his sorrow;
when a Lǔ person mourned at dawn,
Yán Yuān discerned it was a separation in life.
Did these individuals
rely on common sounds for wisdom,
or borrow from musical patterns for verification?
When the heart grieves, the body moves accordingly;
when emotions are sad, the voice expresses sorrow.
This natural correspondence
cannot be escaped.
Only those with divine clarity can master it.
The capable do not find numerous sounds difficult,
nor do the incapable find few sounds easy.
Now, one should not claim that sounds cannot be discerned
simply because they haven't encountered a skilled listener,
or deny that sounds convey sorrow or joy
due to the variability of local customs.
You also say:
'One should not speak of love for the worthy,'
'nor of hatred for the foolish.'
Yet love arises from worthiness,
and hatred forms from foolishness,
only the labels should not be shared.
The expression of sorrow and joy
likewise has its causes.
This means sound makes me sorrowful,
music makes me joyful.
If sorrow and joy come from sound,
then there is substance to it,
so how can both name and reality be dismissed?
You further state:
'Jìzǐ collected poems to observe rites,
distinguishing the Fēng and Yǎ;
Zhòngní praised the consistency of the Sháo music,
thus sighing in admiration.'
What does this mean?
Moreover, when Shī Xiāng performed the melody,
Zhòngní saw King Wén's countenance;
when Shī Juān presented the tune,
Zǐyě recognized the tones of a fallen state.
Did they need to discuss poetry before speaking,
or study rites before making judgments?
These are all divine insights uniquely perceived,
not requiring accumulated days of listening,
yet they grasped the auspicious and inauspicious,
hence former historians regarded them as admirable tales.
Now, with your limited recent knowledge,
you impose boundaries based on what you've seen,
is this not slandering the subtle discernment of past sages,
and betraying the master's exquisite observation?"
The host replied:
"You object that:
though songs and lamentations differ vastly,
skilled listeners naturally perceive them,
without relying on common sounds for wisdom,
or borrowing from musical patterns for verification,
as with Zhōng Zǐ and others.
This means the sorrowful,
even while laughing and dancing,
and the joyful,
even while beating their chests and sighing,
cannot control their outward forms to conceal themselves,
deceiving observers with ambiguity.
You believe that even if sounds are inconsistent,
they should still convey sorrow and joy.
You also say:
'Jìzǐ heard sounds
and knew the customs of various states;
Shī Xiāng performed the melody,
and Zhòngní saw King Wén's countenance.'
According to this,
it means King Wén's virtues and achievements,
and the rise and fall of customs,
can all be symbolized in sound.
The lightness and weight of sounds
can be transmitted to later ages,
and the skill of Xiāng and Juān
can capture them in the future.
If so,
then the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
could exist uninterrupted to this day,
why only these few instances?
If this were true,
then King Wén's melodies would have fixed patterns,
the Sháo and Wǔ music would have set measures,
not mixed with other variations,
nor played with extra notes.
Then your earlier claim of sounds' inconsistency,
and Zhōng Zǐ's analogical understanding,
would be contradicted here.
If sounds are indeed inconsistent,
and Zhōng Zǐ's analogies
are truly valid?
Then Zhòngní's subtle discernment,
and Jì Zhá's skilled listening,
must also be false;
these are all reckless records by vulgar scholars,
attempting to mystify events and fabricate later.
They aim to confuse the world about the way of sound,
not speaking of inherent principles,
but pushing this narrative,
making it divinely obscure and hard to know,
regretting not encountering extraordinary listeners in their time,
admiring ancients and sighing at themselves,
thus greatly deceiving later generations.
To analogize and distinguish things,
one must first seek natural principles.
Once principles are established,
then borrow ancient meanings to clarify them.
Now, without grasping this in heart,
but relying heavily on former words as proof,
from this onward,
I fear even a skilled calculator could not record them.
You also object:
'The expression of sorrow and joy,
is like love and hatred stemming from worthiness and foolishness,
meaning sound makes me sorrowful,
and music makes me joyful.
If sorrow and joy come from sound,
then there is substance to it.'
Now, the five colors have beauty and ugliness,
the five sounds have good and bad,
this is the nature of things.
As for love and non-love,
joy and non-joy,
these changes in human emotion,
and the principles governing things,
stop only here.
Yet none are pre-contained within,
but await external things to form.
As for sorrow and joy, they arise from events,
first encountered in the heart,
only then harmonized with sound
to manifest themselves.
Thus, the previous discussion has clarified their inconsistency,
and now I borrow this talk to rectify names.
I do not say sorrow and joy issue from sound,
as love and hatred arise from worthiness and foolishness.
Rather, harmonious sound moves the human heart,
just as alcohol stirs human nature.
Wine's essence is sweetness or bitterness,
yet the drunkard uses it for joy or anger.
To see joy or sorrow as emitted by sound,
and claim sound has sorrow or joy,
is like seeing joy or anger induced by wine,
and claiming wine possesses the principle of joy or anger."
The Qín guest objected:
"Observing breath and examining color
is universally applicable.
When the heart changes within,
color responds without,
clearly visible,
so you do not doubt it.
Now, sound
is the agitation of breath,
the heart responds to stimuli and moves,
sound follows change and emerges;
the heart has intensity and decline,
sound also rises and falls.
Both are governed by the same body,
why should sound alone be doubted?
If joy and anger are displayed in facial signs,
sorrow and joy should also take form in sound.
Sound naturally has sorrow and joy,
but the ignorant cannot recognize it;
as for Zhōng Zǐ and others,
even encountering inconsistent sounds,
they discerned them with sharp insight.
Now, the blind facing a wall do not comprehend,
while Lí Lóu sees autumn down at a hundred xún;
by this reasoning,
the abilities of the perceptive and ignorant differ.
One cannot hold to a narrow standard
and doubt Lí Lóu's discernment;
cling to mediocre hearing
and suspect Zhōng Zǐ's acuity.
All this is to call the ancients' records false."
The host replied:
"You argue that:
the heart responds to stimuli and moves,
sound follows changes and arises,
the heart has its flourishing and fading,
so sound too has its rises and falls.
Feelings of sorrow and joy
must manifest in sound.
Disciples like Zhōngzǐ,
even when encountering irregular sounds,
would discern them clearly with unique insight.
If it were truly as you say,
then the satiation of Zhuó Zhì,
the starvation at Shǒuyáng,
the injustice of Biàn Hé,
the grief of Bó Qí,
the contained anger of Xiàngrú,
the terror of Bù Zhàn,
in all their thousand changes and hundred forms—
were each to sing a song,
or express themselves through a few notes on the strings,
then disciples like Zhōngzǐ
could each discern their true feelings.
But as listeners,
do you not find it harder to discern with fewer sounds?
And those observing emotions,
do they not treat small and large expressions differently?
If they originate from the same person,
one expects to recognize them.
Suppose the sound comes from below,
then even someone like Zǐyě
would have to take up the pitch pipes and play them
to examine the tones,
discerning the rise and fall of the south wind,
distinguishing the lewdness or correctness of the elegant and vulgar.
Just as eating spicy food and laughing heartily,
or having smoke in the eyes and weeping in sorrow,
both produce tears;
if Dí Yá were to taste them,
he would not claim that tears of joy are sweet
and tears of sorrow are bitter.
This makes it clear.
Why?
Muscular fluids and sweat,
when pressed, flow out effortlessly,
are not governed by sorrow or joy,
much like wine strained through a bag:
though the pressing tools may differ,
the taste of the wine remains unchanged.
Since sounds all emanate from the same body,
why should they uniquely contain the principles of sorrow and joy?
Moreover, the Xiánchí, Liùjīng,
Dàzhāng, Sháoxià—
these were the ultimate music of the ancient kings,
used to move heaven and earth and stir the spirits.
If you insist that sounds invariably reflect their form and convey their heart,
then this ultimate music
could not be entrusted to blind historians;
it must be that sages themselves pluck the strings and pipes,
only then can the elegant music be perfected.
Shùn commanded Kuí to strike and tap the stones,
the eight tones harmonized,
and spirits and humans were in accord.
From this, it follows that
although ultimate music requires sages to create it,
it need not be performed by the sages themselves.
Why?
Because musical sounds possess a natural harmony,
and are not tied to human emotions.
Harmonious music
is achieved through metal and stone;
the most balanced sounds
are obtained from pipes and strings.
Even the finest hair has a form that can be examined,
hence Lí Kuí distinguished between the effects of clarity and obscurity.
If you mix water with water,
how can you tell them apart!"
The guest from Qín objected:
"Although many analogies have hidden flaws,
enough to invite refutation,
the main principle
should hold some validity.
For instance, when Gě Lú heard an ox moo,
he knew its three calves had been sacrificed;
when Shī Kuàng blew the pitch-pipes,
he knew the south wind was weak,
and the Chǔ army would surely be defeated;
when Yángshé's mother heard an infant cry,
she discerned it would bring bereavement to the family.
All these events
were verified in ancient times,
hence they were recorded.
Extrapolating from this,
then prosperity and decline, good and bad fortune,
all reside within sounds.
If you now dismiss this as deceit,
then all previous accounts and records
become discarded objects,
of no use whatsoever.
In terms of a comprehensive theory,
this is hardly acceptable.
If you can clarify the reasons for this,
and illuminate its causes,
while allowing both arguments to stand,
I would like to hear it again in detail."
The host replied:
"I believed that one who could infer three corners from one
grasps the meaning and forgets the words,
hence my previous discussion was brief and not detailed.
Now you trouble me again with the difficulty of circular reasoning,
how dare I not exhaust myself in response?
The Lu ox could foresee its death as a sacrificial animal,
grieved that its three calves no longer existed,
contained sorrow for years,
and poured out its grievances to Gé Lú.
This shows its heart was the same as a human's,
differing only in its beastly form.
This is again what I doubt.
Moreover, oxen are not of humankind,
with no means of communication.
If you claim all birds and beasts can communicate,
and Gé Lú, endowed with special nature,
alone understood them;
this would mean interpreting their calls to discuss events,
akin to translating foreign languages.
If it's not about examining sounds to know their feelings,
then this shouldn't be cited as a difficulty.
If you say a wise person,
upon encountering things, comprehends them,
omnisciently.
Let's first discuss what's easier:
I ask, if a sage suddenly entered barbarian lands,
would he understand their speech?
The challenger must say:
He would.
The reasoning behind this knowledge,
how can it be demonstrated?
I wish to use your objection to establish a criterion for discernment.
Would he recognize their speech through interaction?
Or by blowing pitch-pipes and sounding flutes,
comparing their tones?
Or by observing aura and examining countenance,
to know their hearts?
If knowing the heart
comes freely from aura and countenance,
even without speech,
one could still know it.
The way of knowing
need not rely on words.
If blowing pitch-pipes to compare tones
reveals the heart,
suppose the heart intends a horse,
but mistakenly says deer,
the observer should infer the horse from the deer.
This shows the heart isn't tied to what is said,
and words may not fully attest to the heart.
If understanding speech requires interaction,
this is like a child learning speech from a teacher,
then knowing it,
so what value is there in innate intelligence?
Words are not naturally fixed entities;
different regions have distinct customs,
same things with different names,
casually using one term
as a label.
The sage exhausts principles,
meaning natural principles can be sought,
illuminating even the subtlest,
but if principles are obscured, even the near remains unseen,
thus languages of foreign lands
cannot be forcibly understood.
Extending this logic,
Gé Lú not understanding the ox's bellow
is entirely reasonable, isn't it?
You further object:
Shī Kuàng blew the pitch-pipes,
knew the south wind was not strong,
that Chǔ had many signs of death,
this again is what I doubt.
I ask, when Shī Kuàng blew the pitch-pipes,
was it the wind from Chǔ?
Then a thousand miles apart,
the sound couldn't reach;
if he correctly identified the Chǔ wind,
did it come into the pipes?
Yet south of Chǔ are Wú and Yuè,
north are Liáng and Sòng,
if he didn't see its origin,
how could he recognize it?
Generally, yin and yang clash,
then form wind;
the interaction of energies
touches the ground and arises.
How could it arise in the Chǔ court
and come to Jìn?
Moreover, the pitch-pipes divide the energies of the four seasons;
when the season comes, energy moves,
the pipes respond, and the ashes shift,
all naturally corresponding,
not relying on human intervention.
Generating upper and lower tones
serves to balance the harmony of the five notes,
and order the distinction between hard and soft.
Yet the pipes have fixed sounds;
even if blowing Zhōnglǚ in winter,
its tone remains full and undiminished.
Now, with a Jìn person's breath,
blowing the unresponsive pipes,
how could the Chǔ wind enter them
and cause expansion or contraction?
Wind has no form,
sound and pipes do not communicate;
thus, in assessing principles,
there's no basis in wind or pipes,
isn't that so?
Could it be that Shī Kuàng, being knowledgeable and erudite,
naturally knew the signs of victory and defeat,
and to secure the people's hearts,
attributed it to mystical subtlety,
like Bó Cháng Qiān deceiving Duke Jìng about longevity?
You also object:
Yángshé's mother heard an infant cry
and discerned it would bring bereavement to the family.
Again, I ask, how did she know?
Was it divine intuition alone,
暗语而當耶?
Had she heard a cry before,
similarly loud and ominous,
and the current cry
resembled the past one?
So she knew it meant family loss?
If it was divine intuition,
a dark utterance that proved correct,
it wasn't derived from reasoning.
Though called listening to the cry,
it didn't draw evidence from the infant's sound.
If she judged the sound as ominous based on past experience,
thus knowing the present cry was ominous,
this is using sound A as a standard
to measure cry B.
The relation of sound to tone
is like that of form to heart.
There are forms alike but sentiments different,
appearances dissimilar but hearts alike.
How to clarify this?
Sages share similar hearts and virtues,
yet their forms differ.
If hearts are alike but forms different,
why speak of observing form to know the heart?
Moreover, the mouth pushing air to make sound
is no different from reeds drawing air to whistle.
The goodness or badness of a cry
doesn't come from the infant's mouth being auspicious or ominous,
just as the clarity or muddiness of a zither
isn't due to the player's skill.
The heart can distinguish principles and argue well,
but cannot make the inner reed pipe smooth;
like a blind musician can master the melody,
but cannot ensure the instrument is clear and harmonious.
The instrument doesn't rely on a skilled blind player to be good,
nor the pipe on a wise heart to be tuned.
Thus, the heart and sound
are clearly two separate things.
If two things are indeed distinct,
then those seeking sentiment shouldn't focus on observing forms,
and those gauging hearts shouldn't rely on listening to sounds.
Observers wanting to know the heart through sound
are being external, aren't they?
Now, the Jìn mother hadn't gained this from experience,
but solely trusted a past sound
to judge the present cry;
wasn't this mistakenly hitting upon what earlier curious minds
then praised?"
The Qín guest objected:
"I've heard the defeated aren't ashamed to flee,
for it preserves them.
My heart is not yet weary,
and I raise another difficulty,
returning to the remainder.
Now, peaceful people,
hearing zhēng, flute, or pipa,
become physically agitated and spirited;
hearing zither or se melodies,
they listen quietly with tranquil hearts.
In the same instrument,
different pieces vary,
and emotions change accordingly:
playing Qín tunes brings admiration and fervor,
performing Qí or Chǔ music unifies feelings and focuses thoughts,
playing delicate ditties brings joy and satisfaction.
The heart changes with the sound,
in so many ways.
If agitation and calm come from sound,
why limit it to sorrow and joy?
Yet you only say perfectly harmonious sounds
can move all things,
attributing great unity to sound,
reducing all changes to human emotion;
isn't this knowing that without understanding this?"
The host replied:
"You argue:
'Pipa, zheng, and flutes
make people restless and excited.
You also say:
'As the music varies,
so do emotions change accordingly.'
This indeed explains why music constantly moves people.
Pipa, zheng, and flutes
have close intervals and high pitches,
with numerous variations and rapid rhythms.
Using high pitches to control frequent rhythmic changes
thus causes
people's bodies to become restless and their spirits excited,
just as bells alarm the ears
and drums startle the heart.
Therefore, when hearing the sound of war drums,
one thinks of military commanders;
this is because sounds have different volumes,
thus affecting people with either intensity or calmness.
The nature of qin and se
features wide intervals and low pitches,
with sparse variations and pure sounds.
Using low pitches to govern infrequent changes,
if one does not listen with an open and calm mind,
one cannot fully appreciate the ultimate clarity and harmony,
thus listening brings tranquility and mental ease.
The different uses of music
are like the distinct sounds of different instruments.
The melodies of Qí and Chǔ are mostly profound,
thus emotions become unified;
their variations are subtle,
thus concentration becomes focused.
The music of exquisite melodies
gathers the beauty of all sounds,
combining the harmony of the five tones,
its substance is rich and its application broad,
thus the mind is engaged with multiple principles;
when the five tones converge,
joy is released and desires satisfied.
Yet all are based on the qualities of simplicity, complexity, high, low, good, and bad,
while human emotions respond with restlessness, calm, focus, or distraction.
It is like wandering through a marketplace,
where the eyes become overwhelmed and emotions unrestrained;
whereas contemplating musical patterns
brings calm thoughts and dignified demeanor.
This shows that the nature of sound
lies entirely in tempo;
emotional responses to sound
are limited to restlessness and calmness.
Though the uses of music vary,
and emotions change accordingly,
it is like different delicious flavors
that the mouth can distinguish.
The five tastes may vary immensely,
yet all share the quality of deliciousness;
musical variations may be numerous,
yet all share the quality of harmony.
Deliciousness has sweetness,
harmony has pleasure;
yet emotions following music
are fully contained within the realm of harmony;
the mouth responding to deliciousness
is confined within the boundary of sweetness.
How can sorrow or joy exist within them?
However, people's emotions differ,
each according to their understanding,
thus expressing what lies within.
If one speaks of equanimity where sorrow and joy are balanced,
then nothing takes precedence to be expressed,
thus ultimately only restlessness or calmness is attained.
If something is expressed,
then there is something dominant within,
not equanimity.
From this perspective,
restlessness and calmness
are the effects of sound;
sorrow and joy
are the masters of emotion;
one cannot see that sound evokes responses of restlessness or calmness
and therefore claim that sorrow and joy both originate from sound.
Moreover, although sounds may have intensity or calmness,
each intensity and calmness possesses its own harmony,
and what harmony evokes
all arises spontaneously from within.
How to illustrate this?
When guests fill the hall,
and wine flows freely as the qin is played,
some may rejoice with happiness,
while others may weep with sorrow,
not because sorrow is conveyed to one
or joy guided to another.
The music remains unchanged from before,
yet joy and sorrow simultaneously appear—
is this not like the myriad differences in nature's breath?
Precisely because there is no inherent master of joy or anger,
there should also be no inherent master of sorrow or joy,
thus both joy and sorrow manifest.
If music were inherently biased
and contained uniform sounds,
its expressions would each fit their categories,
then how could it universally engage all principles
and evoke the emotions of all?
Hence, it can be said:
Sound takes equanimity as its essence,
yet its influence on things is not fixed;
the heart and mind rely on what is awaited within,
responding to stimuli and then expressing.
Thus, sound and the heart
follow different paths and tracks,
not interweaving with each other—
how could they stain supreme harmony with joy or sorrow,
or attach empty labels of grief and happiness?"
The guest from Qín objected:
"Your argument states:
'Intense and calm sounds
each have their own harmony,
and what harmony evokes
all arises spontaneously from within.'
Thus, when wine flows freely and the qin is played,
both joy and sorrow appear.
This means that biased emotions
first accumulate within,
so those harboring joy encounter sorrowful sounds and express it,
while those with inner sorrow meet joyful music and are moved.
Surely music inherently possesses definite sorrow or joy,
but musical influence is gradual,
cannot be rushed,
and cannot be swapped.
Biased emotions
are triggered upon contact with things,
thus causing sorrow and joy to respond simultaneously.
Even if both emotions appear,
how does this damage the principle that sound has fixed qualities?"
The host replied:
"You argue:
'Sorrow and joy inherently reside in fixed sounds,
but biased emotions
cannot be instantly altered,
thus those with sorrow encounter joyful music and still feel sorrow.'
If it is as you say,
that sound has fixed attributes,
suppose 'The Deer Cry' is played repeatedly—
this is joyful music—
yet someone sorrowful hears it.
Although musical influence is gradual,
it should merely be unable to make them change to joy;
why would it instead increase their sorrow?
It is like a single torch flame:
although it cannot warm a whole room,
it should not increase the coldness.
For fire is not something that intensifies cold,
nor is joyful music a tool that enhances sorrow.
When strings are played in a grand hall,
and both joy and sorrow appear,
it is precisely because perfect harmony releases pent-up feelings and guides emotions,
thus allowing what is stirred by external things
to express itself fully.
You argue:
'Biased emotions
are triggered upon contact with things,
thus causing sorrow and joy to respond simultaneously.'
When speaking of sorrow,
some weep upon seeing a table and staff,
some grieve upon witnessing a carriage or garment.
Simply because they are moved by the person's absence while the object remains,
paining over the evident event and the hidden form.
The reasons for their feelings
all have their own causes,
not that sorrow arises wherever they touch,
or tears flow wherever they sit.
Now, without a table or staff to stir feelings,
yet tears flow upon hearing harmonious sounds—
is this not because what harmony evokes
all arises spontaneously from within?"
Qínkè objected, saying:
"The argument states:
When wine flows freely and the qín is played,
both joy and sorrow arise.
To clarify this statement,
you responded by citing partial emotions,
claiming they are stirred by external stimuli.
Now let us speak from the heart,
and demonstrate with tangible effects.
The human heart, if not joyful, is sorrowful;
if not sorrowful, then joyful—
this defines the broad realm of emotional disposition.
Now weeping is the injury of sorrow,
while laughter is the expression of joy.
I have heard that those who listen to Qí and Chǔ melodies
only exhibit tearful countenances,
and have never been seen with laughing visages.
This must mean Qí and Chǔ melodies take sorrow as their essence,
thus what they evoke
all corresponds to their measure.
How could it merely be that multiple repetitions with little variation
lead to concentrated emotions and focused thoughts?
If they can truly induce weeping,
then that sound possesses sorrowfulness—
this can be decisively known."
The host replied:
"Although human emotions are moved to sorrow or joy,
the degrees of sorrow and joy vary;
moreover, the extremes of sorrow and joy
need not manifest identically.
Minor sorrow shows in disturbed composure,
deep grief leads to weeping—
this is the way of sorrow.
Minor joy brings a cheerful face,
supreme joy creates heartfelt delight—
this is the principle of joy.
How to illustrate this?
When with beloved ones in peaceful comfort,
one is serene as if natural,
being self-content.
But when in dire crisis,
barely rescued thereafter,
one claps hands but does not dance.
From this perspective,
dancing cannot match the former self-contentment—
is this not indeed so?
As for loud laughter,
though it springs from joyful feeling,
it forms through reasoning;
it is not a natural, sound-responsive instrument.
This shows that joy's response to sound
takes self-contentment as its core;
while sorrow's response to stimulus
takes shedding tears as its mark.
Tears falling involve physical movement that can be perceived,
self-contentment involves spiritual harmony without outward change.
Thus observing their differences,
one fails to recognize their similarities;
distinguishing their external manifestations,
one overlooks their internal essence.
Yet laughter's non-appearance in sound
is hardly unique to Qí and Chǔ melodies.
Now if you do not seek joy in the realm of self-contentment,
but equate absence of laughter with Qí and Chǔ's sorrowful essence,
is this not recognizing sorrow while failing to understand joy?"
Qínkè inquired further:[70"Confucius once said:
'To transform customs and practices,
nothing is better than music.'
If as you argue,
all sorrow and joy
reside not in sound,
then how indeed
can customs be transformed?
Moreover, the ancients cautioned against decadent trends
and restrained ears-dazzling music,
hence saying:
'Banish the music of Zhèng,
keep away glib talkers.'
Then how could the tunes of Zhèng and Wèi,
played on sounding stones to harmonize spirits and humans...
I dare ask: between Zhèng and Yǎ's essences,
their rise and decline reaching extremes,
by what means can customs transformation be achieved?
I beg to hear again,
to resolve my doubts."
The host responded, saying:
"Those who speak of transforming customs and mores
must inherit an era of decline and decay.
The ancient kings,
receiving the Mandate of Heaven to govern all things,
necessarily honored simple and easy teachings,
practicing governance through non-action.
The ruler remained tranquil above,
ministers were compliant below,
mysterious transformations silently permeated,
Heaven and humanity interacted in harmony.
Withered things of all kinds
were bathed in spiritual dew,
within the six directions,
all were cleansed in the great flow,
washed free of dust and grime;
all living beings rested in comfort,
each seeking abundant blessings for themselves;
silently following the Way,
embracing loyalty and upholding righteousness,
without even realizing how it came to be so.
When harmonious hearts are content within,
harmonious energy manifests without,
thus songs are used to express aspirations,
dances to proclaim emotions.
Afterward, they are adorned with elegant patterns,
illuminated with the spirit of the Odes,
disseminated through the eight tones,
influenced by the Great Harmony,
guiding their spiritual energy,
nurturing it to completion.
Meeting their innate dispositions,
bringing them to clarity;
causing hearts to accord with principle,
energy to correspond with sound,
harmonizing in convergence,
thereby perfecting their beauty.
Thus feelings of joyful music
appear in metal and stone instruments;
the encompassing and radiant virtue
manifests in tones and melodies.
If this is practiced, then all states share the same customs,
fragrant blossoms flourish abundantly,
sweet as autumn orchids,
achieving trust without appointment,
accomplishment without planning,
serenely loving one another,
like unfolding brocade and displaying splendor,
brilliant and dazzling to behold.
The flourishing of the Great Way
reaches its peak here,
the task of great peace
finds its ultimate manifestation here.
Therefore it is said:
'For transforming customs and mores,
nothing is better than music.'
The essence of music
takes the heart as its master.
Thus soundless music
is the parent of the people.
As for the harmonious blending of the eight tones,
which brings people joy,
this too is collectively called music.
However, the transformation of customs
does not fundamentally lie here.
The harmonious blending of tones
is something human emotions cannot resist.
Therefore the ancients, knowing emotions cannot be let loose,
restrained what would lead them astray;
knowing desires cannot be extinguished,
followed their natural origins.
They established rituals that could be upheld,
created music that could guide.
Mouths did not indulge in all flavors,
music did not exhaust all sounds,
measuring what was appropriate from start to finish,
gauging the mean between wise and foolish;
establishing standards for it,
so that near and far shared the same customs,
using it without exhaustion,
thereby also cementing loyalty and trust,
manifesting what does not change.
Thus village schools and academies followed accordingly,
causing strings and bamboos to coexist with ritual vessels,
feathers and ceremonial postures to be used together,
proper speech and harmonious sounds to issue forth simultaneously.
So that those about to hear these sounds
would necessarily hear these words;
those about to observe these appearances
would necessarily honor these rituals.
Ritual is like the host and guest ascending and descending,
after which toasts are exchanged.
Thereupon the rhythm of speech,
the measure of sound,
the ceremony of bowing and yielding,
the pattern of movement and stillness,
advancing and withdrawing complement each other,
together forming one body.
Ruler and minister used them at court,
common scholars used them at home.
Learning them young,
they did not neglect them when grown,
hearts at peace, wills firm,
daily moving toward goodness,
then approaching them with reverence,
maintaining them long without change,
only then was transformation achieved,
this again was the ancient kings' intent in using music.
Therefore in court banquets and diplomatic ceremonies,
excellent music was always present,
so the state historians collected information on the rise and fall of customs,
entrusted it to the musicians,
expressed it through pipes and strings,
ensuring those who spoke were without guilt,
and those who heard had sufficient warning,
this again was the ancient kings' intent in using music.
As for the music of Zhèng,
it represents the ultimate in musical artistry,
such exquisite music moves people,
just as beautiful looks delude the will,
excessive indulgence and unrestrained drinking
easily lead to loss of vocation.
Unless one is a perfect person,
who can withstand it?
The ancient kings feared the world would drift away without return,
so while possessing the eight tones,
they did not profane their sounds,
preserved their great harmony,
without exhausting their variations.
They moderated seductive melodies,
making music joyful but not licentious,
like the grand sacrifice broth without seasoning,
not reaching the extreme of spiciness.
If flowing into shallow vulgarity,
then the sounds would lack sufficient pleasure,
nor would they be enjoyable.
If those above lose the Way,
the state loses its order,
men and women elope and follow,
licentious and unrestrained without measure,
then customs change accordingly,
mores form according to preferences.
If what they aspire to is exalted,
then all abilities will indulge it;
if they delight in their habits,
how can they be reproved?
Relying on harmonious sounds,
matching and extending them,
sincerity stirred by words,
hearts moved by harmony,
once customs are formed,
they are named accordingly.
Yet the sounds thus named
contain nothing licentious or depraved.
The licentious and the proper alike reside in the heart,
the forms of the Yǎ and Zhèng
are also sufficient for observation."
Discussion on Abandoning Self-Interest
A gentleman is one
whose mind does not dwell on right and wrong,
yet whose actions do not deviate from the Way.
Why is this said?
For those with tranquil energy and empty spirit,
their minds harbor no arrogance;
those with enlightened bodies and open hearts,
their emotions are not bound by desires.
With no arrogance in mind,
they transcend conventional teachings and follow nature;
with emotions unbound by desires,
they discern nobility and baseness, understanding the nature of things.
When the nature of things is smoothly understood,
the great Way is not violated;
transcending conventions and following the heart,
thus right and wrong are not dwelled upon.
Therefore, speaking of a gentleman,
they prioritize non-dwelling,
and value understanding things.
Speaking of petty persons,
they consider concealing emotions wrong,
and view deviating from the Way as a flaw.
Why?
Concealing emotions and boasting of goodness
are the worst traits of petty persons;
an open heart without dwelling
is the sincere conduct of a gentleman.
Thus, the great Way says,
"When I have no self,"
"What have I to worry about?"
Not valuing life itself
is better than prizing life.
From this perspective,
the way the ultimate person uses their mind
inherently does not involve dwelling.
Thus, Yī Yǐn did not hesitate to be virtuous under Yīn Tāng,
so his legacy flourished and his name shone.
Zhōu Dàn did not avoid suspicion and acted covertly,
hence his regency elevated transformation.
Yí Wú did not hide his feelings from Qí Huán,
so the state became hegemonic and the ruler respected.
In their use of mind,
how could they be tied to selfishness for their own sake?
Thus Guǎnzǐ said:
"A gentleman practices the Way,
forgetting it is for themselves."
This saying is correct.
A gentleman's virtuous actions
are not executed after measuring their propriety.
Following the heart without evil,
they do not debate goodness before acting rightly.
Revealing emotions without dwelling,
they do not discuss rightness before acting.
Thus, loftily forgetting virtue,
yet virtue aligns with measure;
spontaneously following the heart,
and the heart meets goodness;
unexpectedly not dwelling,
and affairs coincide with rightness.
Therefore, discussing public and private,
even if one intends the Way and preserves goodness,
and lacks evil,
but harbors and conceals nothing,
cannot be called without private motives;
even if one boasts of goodness,
and emotions violate the Way,
but holds nothing unexpressed,
cannot be called not public.
Now, insisting on absolute public principle
to judge private feelings,
makes even those who do good
not free from selfishness;
even those who boast of goodness
not fall into being unpublic,
emphasizing their name and valuing their heart,
then the reality of right and wrong
cannot but be revealed.
When right and wrong are clearly revealed,
the good have no hidden faults,
the wrongdoers bear no great accusation of being unpublic,
with no faults, goodness is fully achieved,
with no great wrongs, errors are merely errors,
which is how errors are remedied.
Not only achieving full goodness,
but also reforming the ungood.
Goodness to perfect goodness,
criticism to correct faults,
especially with ultimate right and wrong.
Thus good and ungood
are extremes among things.
If placed between these two,
where one goes,
public leads to success, private to failure.
Using the same vessel,
some succeed, some fail.
Public and private
are paths to success or failure,
and gates to fortune or misfortune.
Thus, few remain unchanged when things reach extremes,
many are applied before reaching extremes.
If based on the average person's nature,
operating with usable qualities,
and dwelling on ancient virtues,
stepping onto the public path, speaking from the heart,
then words are all right,
acting on genuine feelings,
then affairs are all auspicious.
In this case, what is dwelled upon
is not what should be dwelled upon;
what is privately desired
is not what should be private.
Speaking without calculating gain or loss yet meeting goodness,
acting without measuring right and wrong yet encountering fortune,
is this the rule of public success and private failure?
If so,
what is there to dwell upon?
Thus, Lǐ Fú exposed theft,
Jìn Wén was amiable;
Bó Dī confessed guilt,
loyalty established, life preserved.
Miù Xián disclosed fault,
his words accepted, reputation praised;
Jiàn Lí expressed sincerity,
the whole hall wept,
yet these men all faced mortal danger,
confronted unforeseeable crises,
revealed their hearts and minds,
and still remained safe;
how much more for a gentleman without their crimes,
but with their goodness?
The act of dwelling on goodness
is their ailment.
Only by treating the ailment
can one be free from ailment;
being ill but able to cure it
is better than being ill.
Yet some things appear wrong but are not wrong,
seem right but are not right,
which must be examined.
Thus, in the pivot of adaptation,
some boast to achieve humility,
greed to attain integrity,
folly to form wisdom,
tolerance to aid benevolence.
But in moments of boastfulness,
one cannot be called without integrity;
in forms of suspicion and tolerance,
one cannot be called without benevolence.
This is seeming wrong but not wrong.
Some slander seems trustworthy,
but cannot be called sincere;
provoked theft seems loyal,
but cannot be called public.
This is seeming right but not right.
Therefore, judge by their intentions,
determine their direction,
hold their words to gauge their reasoning,
examine their feelings to trace changes,
follow from the start,
name the end.
Then, those with selfish motives
cannot use seeming wrong to excuse their wrongs;
those with pure hearts
cannot tread on seeming right to bear their rightness.
Thus, true right may briefly seem wrong before revealing itself,
true wrong may briefly seem right before becoming clear.
When public and private are both evident,
the selfish have nothing to hope for,
and the pure-hearted have nothing to bear.
The selfish having no hope
leads them to reconsider their wrongs;
the public-minded having no fear
allows them to act without doubt.
This is the way of great order.
Thus, the concubine overturned the wine,
and was executed for the crime;
Wáng Líng disputed at court,
while Chén Píng complied with the decree.
From this we see,
are these not cases of seeming wrong but not wrong?
Clarifying the sincere conduct of a gentleman,
revealing where public and private lie,
filling the hall and steps,
all eyes watching,
and saying:
"They are good people."
Yet those who turn away and privately discuss with hidden motives
are not in harmony.
Those clinging to bias and concealing feelings unaltered,
truly have spirits lost in confusion,
and bodies drowned in conventional fame.
Hearts constrained by fear,
and emotions tied to desires.
All consider themselves right,
and none wiser than themselves.
Without the agony of physical pain,
or the shock of heart-wrenching disaster,
they cannot retract emotions to reflect,
nor abandon fame to embrace reality.
Thus, the heart has its rightness,
Concealing it out of selfishness;
intentions may be good,
yet actions turn to evil.
Not acting where one should act,
but acting where one should not;
not seeking the reason for not acting,
but pursuing the way to act.
Thus, one appears to act wisely,
but is blind to true action,
hence regarding non-action as clumsy,
and forced action as skillful.
Only fearing that concealment is not subtle enough,
only worrying that secrecy is not tight enough.
Thus, putting on a solemn demeanor,
to impress ordinary people;
using hypocritical words,
to seek vulgar praise.
Claiming that the best plan for longevity,
is nothing greater than this;
spending all day in restless thought,
never looking beyond it.
Thus, they achieve the form of their selfishness,
but lose their natural essence.
Therefore, feelings of concealment,
must reside in the heart;
the mechanisms of pretense and negligence,
must manifest in affairs.
If so,
then discussions of right and wrong become clear,
and the reality of rewards and punishments becomes firm.
Not knowing that staying in shade can avoid shadows,
but worrying that shadows are not hidden,
not knowing that non-action can avoid troubles,
but worrying about acting improperly—is this not lamentable!
Thus, Shēnhóu flattered and complied,
only to be abandoned by Chǔ Gōng;
Zǎi Pǐ indulged in selfishness,
and ultimately suffered disaster.
From this, it is said,
none who cling to concealment and selfishness,
can stand upright in a clear age;
none who hide wrongs and conceal feelings,
can establish trust and a renowned name.
The noble person already possesses the essence,
and also observes the mirror.
Valuing openness and clarity,
they display and preserve it;
despising arrogance and stinginess,
they discard and distance it.
If a single action is wrong,
they feel inner shame before the spirit;
if a hidden flaw is exposed,
they feel outer shame in their form.
Words without careless taboos,
and actions without careless concealment.
Not deeming something good out of favoritism,
nor deeming something wrong out of aversion.
The heart holds no arrogance,
and emotions bear no attachments,
the body pure and spirit upright,
thus judgments of right and wrong are fair.
Loyalty moves the enlightened Son of Heaven,
and trust is firm among the myriad people.
Placing aspirations across the eight wildernesses,
radiating openness and magnanimity throughout the days.
Is this not the noble and extraordinary conduct,
of virtuous and noble individuals?
Someone asked:
Did Dìwǔ Lún have selfishness?
He replied:
Once, my elder brother's son was ill,
I visited ten times in one night, yet slept peacefully upon return.
When my own son was ill,
I did not visit all morning,
but could not sleep the entire night.
Can this be called selfishness?
Or not?
The answer was:
This is a matter of right and wrong,
not selfishness.
Selfishness takes not speaking as its name,
public-mindedness takes full disclosure as its mark,
goodness takes lack of intent as its essence,
wrong takes forced action as its burden.
Now Dìwǔ Lún revealed his feelings,
this is selflessness;
his anxiety over not visiting and sleeplessness,
indicates a sense of wrong.
To be selfless yet acknowledge wrong,
is the mindset of non-action.
Those who speak of non-action,
do not insist on total expression;
those who speak with much reserve,
are not merely about not speaking.
Thus, much reserve may involve wrong,
while non-action may involve right.
However, the reason non-action can be right,
lies in having no exalted ambitions,
no desires in the heart,
understanding the nature of the great Way,
acting with spontaneity,
then there is no path to wrong.
Embracing unity without forced action,
then there is no selfishness.
Absence of wrong combined with these two principles,
constitutes supreme beauty.
If one can speak of wrong,
this is better than silent selfishness,
not the greater wrong of being emotionless.
Now Dìwǔ Lún acknowledged wrong and revealed it,
which cannot be said not public-minded.
The right and wrong he revealed,
cannot be said to be forced action.
To call acknowledgment of wrong selfish,
cannot be said not confused.
Such is the principle of public and private.
An Essay on Guǎnshū and Càishū
Someone asked:
'According to records,
Guǎnshū and Càishū spread rumors,
and rebelled in the Eastern Capital.
The Duke of Zhōu launched a campaign,
punishing them for their treachery,
their stubborn evil clearly evident,
their names condemned for millennia.
Moreover, their enlightened father and sage brother,
failed to discern their vicious folly in youth,
recognize them as unworthy子弟,
yet entrusted them with governing the troubled people of Yīn,
granting them honors and titles in feudal states,
allowing evils to accumulate and crimes to form,
until they met with calamity.
This defies logic,
and leaves the heart unsettled.
I wish to hear an explanation.'
The reply said:
"Excellent is your question.
In the past, King Wén and King Wǔ employed Guǎnshū and Càishū based on their substance,
while the Duke of Zhōu executed Guǎnshū and Càishū as a matter of expediency.
Expedient actions are evident,
while substantial principles remain submerged.
Hence, people of the time simplistically label Guǎnshū and Càishū as stubborn and wicked,
so I shall now discuss this for you.
Now, Guǎnshū and Càishū both submitted to instruction and died for righteousness,
their loyalty and sincerity being natural,
thus King Wén ranked them and made them prominent,
while the two sages, King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu,
raised and employed them,
not out of personal affection or favoritism;
rather, it was to honor virtue and respect worthies,
to rescue the troubled people of Yīn,
to pacify and assist Wǔ Gēng,
and to uplift the stubborn customs,
achieving merit in their tasks,
thus their legacy remained unabolished for generations,
their names topped their time,
and they were ranked as feudal lords.
When it came to King Wǔ's death,
his heir, King Chéng, being young and immature,
the Duke of Zhōu assumed governance,
leading the feudal lords in court,
aspiring to glorify the former records,
and to elevate the royal enterprise.
However, Guǎnshū and Càishū, though submitting to instruction,
failed to comprehend the sage's expediency,
suddenly encountered great changes,
and could not extricate themselves.
Loyal in their hearts,
thinking of the royal house,
they then raised their voices and led the masses,
wishing to eliminate the state's calamity,
to protect the Son of Heaven,
even willing to destroy the Duke of Zhōu.
This was the outburst of foolish sincerity,
which led to their seeking disaster.
King Chéng greatly awakened,
the Duke of Zhōu was restored to prominence,
unifying transformations and standardizing customs,
righteousness cutting off personal affection;
although internally trusting as in their hearts,
externally their stance was untenable,
raising troops in rebellion,
misleading many.
Therefore, with restraint, punishment was administered,
executing them with tears,
demonstrating rewards and punishments,
not avoiding relatives.
Honors and ranks displayed
must concentrate on great virtue;
punishments and floggings applied
must befall the guilty.
This is the correct form of teaching,
the clear principle of past and present.
Although Guǎnshū and Càishū harbored loyalty and sincerity,
they were ultimately guilty and executed,
their guilt and execution being evident,
they cannot be reexamined.
Internally, they must remain obscure,
their crimes thus manifest.
The paths of obscurity and manifestation greatly differ,
hence through generations, they have not been exonerated.
Yet commentators, accepting names and trusting actions,
readily deem Guǎnshū and Càishū evil,
not realizing that labeling Guǎnshū and Càishū evil
implies that the three sages were unwise.
If the three sages were not unwise,
then sages would not support evil or employ the stubborn and wicked.
The stubborn and wicked are not tolerated in an enlightened age,
thus Guǎnshū and Càishū gained no favor from their father and brother,
and being appointed, they must have been loyal and good,
so the two uncles were originally virtuous and good.
Now, if based on the three sages' use of wisdom and thought for prominence,
granting them substantial principles,
inferring the obscure expediency of the loyal and worthy,
discussing the great principles of statecraft,
then the goodness of the two uncles becomes evident,
the three sages' employment of them had reason,
the spread of rumors had cause,
and the Duke of Zhōu's execution was justified.
Moreover, when the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent,
Shào Gōng was displeased.
Inferring from this,
then Guǎnshū and Càishū's doubts,
were not necessarily unworthy,
and the loyal and worthy may not comprehend expediency;
the three sages did not employ evil,
yet the Duke of Zhōu had to execute them.
If so,
the three sages employed truly good men,
the Duke of Zhōu's execution was appropriate,
and the hearts of Guǎnshū and Càishū are understood.
Then the great righteousness is comprehended,
both external and internal aspects are accounted for,
without mutual contradiction,
and contemporary discussions can also be relieved and greatly resolved."
One Essay on Wisdom and Courage
There was a Master Lǚ,
who delved into essence and savored the Way,
scrutinizing right and wrong,
believing that a person can have courage without wisdom,
but having wisdom entails having courage.
Master Jī contended that wisdom and courage have distinct functions,
and cannot generate each other.
The essay states:
"Now, the primal energy molds and tempers,
and all living beings receive from it.
What is endowed varies in amount,
hence talents and natures have dullness and brightness.
Only the supreme person is endowed with pure beauty,
comprehensive both internally and externally,
lacking nothing, fully equipped,
below this level,
there are deficiencies.
Some are clear in perceiving things,
some are brave in making decisions.
Human inclinations towards greed or integrity,
each have their limits,
akin to plants and trees,
categorized and distinct.
Those who combine both are broad in dealing with things,
those biased in endowment guard their share.
Therefore, I say wisdom and courage stem from different energies,
and cannot generate each other.
Wisdom is for perceiving things,
courage is for making decisions,
with only wisdom and no courage,
one may see but not decide,
with only courage and no wisdom,
one acts contrary to reason and misses opportunities.
Hence, Zǐ Jiā's weakness
led to his implication in regicide;
Zuǒ Shī's indecision
saw him pressured by Huà Chén.
Both had the wisdom but failed to act decisively.
This principle is evident,
leaving no room for doubt.
Thus, I briefly illustrate one aspect,
hoping to avoid further doubt."
Lǚ Zǐ said:
"I have respectfully perused your discourse,
which may be called an ocean that cannot be increased.
Analyzing principles values conciseness and thorough expression of feelings,
why indulge in verbose and far-fetched absurdities?
Now your argument
invokes the primordial chaos as a metaphor,
how distant and vague it is!
Therefore, I shall directly respond with the practical essentials of human affairs.
Jiǎ Yì of the Hàn dynasty,
presented straightforward strategies,
exerting the utmost in critical speech.
He implemented them without hesitation,
demonstrating his clarity of perception.
His fear of the owl led him to compose a rhapsody,
revealing his obscured confusion.
Can one person's courage
truly wax and wane?
It is a matter of seeing or not seeing,
hence the decisiveness in action varies.
Zǐ Jiā and Zuǒ Shī,
both foolish and shallow in their shortcomings,
lacked thorough understanding,
thus they were confused by ambiguities,
ultimately meeting with disaster.
Was it not due to a lack of decisive courage despite clear insight?
Thus, Huò Guāng, possessing deep bravery,
undertook the responsibilities of a high general,
and contended in the affairs of Wáng Hè.
Yánnián Wénshēng,
though previously without military acclaim,
proposed righteous ideas and fervent words,
his courage soaring above the clouds,
this is evidence of it.
As for Yú Qī offering his head,
and Líng's mother falling on her sword,
those of clear determination,
such examples are countless,
to detail and record them all,
would be an endless task.
Moreover, there are those who see a smooth path but dare not set foot on it,
or who, at the steps to the clouded path, doubt reaching the great purity.
If foolish and flawed individuals are capable,
entrusting themselves to obscurity,
abandoning themselves in pitfalls,
like Dào Zhī hiding in the tiger's mouth,
or thieves leading with their heads in ditches,
and those who rashly confront tigers or cross rivers,
the foolish and daring types,
then such can exist.
Therefore, I say clarity without courage,
and courage without partial steadfastness,
are easily understood principles,
not requiring many analogies.
Hence, I won't cite extensive words from afar.
If you haven't grasped the broader implications,
and still have doubts,
I hope to receive further instruction,
to fully express my views."
"Discussing the nature of reason and emotions,
analyzing similarities and differences,
indeed one should trace the origins of what is received,
and deduce the sources of innate dispositions.
Following the beginning to reach the end,
only then can one avoid contradictions.
Now you wish to discard the primordial chaos,
picking only from what you see,
this is like favoring the mesh of a net,
while disliking holding the main rope.
The fundamental argument is that the two energies differ,
clarity does not generate courage,
to thoroughly discuss this,
one should consider a person who spreads criticism without the courage to satirize,
yet has the clarity to perceive affairs.
Thus, there will inevitably be harm from indecision.
It's not that the blood and energy of an average person
lack it and then restore it,
but by supplementing it with clarity,
the two energies coexist in one body,
then clarity can mobilize courage,
as seen in Jiǎ Yì.
Jiǎ Yì's clarity and courage,
sufficiently complemented each other,
hence he could accomplish tasks.
Who says he entirely lacked courage,
relying solely on clarity to act?
You alone make this statement,
to fit your argument.
His fear of the owl was due to obscured confusion,
a gap in his clarity,
how does it harm his courage?
Once clarity perceives things,
courage enables action.
If clarity does not see,
what can courage decide?
They support each other in advance and retreat,
can this be called waxing and waning?
Based on this reasoning,
Jiǎ Yì presenting strategies,
was due to his clarity of sight;
his fear of the owl leading to a rhapsody,
was due to obscured confusion.
How could he be clear-sighted before,
and confused later?
It shows that clarity has its fluctuations;
if clarity can advance and retreat,
why can't courage be partial?
You acknowledge that Huò Guāng had deep bravery,
yet he struggled in deposing the king,
this indicates his bravery was somewhat hindered.
And you say one person's courage cannot wax and wane,
this is correct.
Jiǎ Yì's fear of the owl,
was due to a blockage in his clarity.
Huò Guāng's fear in the deposition,
was a hindrance to his bravery.
Only the utmost clarity can be free from confusion,
and the utmost courage can be without deficiency.
Unless one is like this,
who is without flaws and losses?
But we should generally consider the broad outline of presence and absence,
and proceed with the discussion.
Matters are primarily judged by tangible evidence,
Yánnián's fervor,
his bravery and righteousness soaring above the clouds,
this is courage.
Yet you say he previously had no military reputation,
this is trusting past claims over doubting achieved deeds.
Yánnián in deliberation,
demonstrated his clarity of insight.
His vigorous spirit soaring fiercely,
is the decisiveness of courage.
This is sufficient to observe.
You also say:
that clarity without courage,
and courage without partial steadfastness.
Examining your words,
this implies that a person with specialized courage
also possesses courage as a distinct energy.
The five elements exist in the body,
each generating its own.
Clarity arises from the brightness of yang,
courage from the consolidation of yin.
How can one have yang and generate yin,
or be without yang?
Although they rely on each other to combine virtues,
they essentially originate from different energies.
As for the various other arguments,
about Yú Qī, Líng's mother, confronting tigers, and so on,
thousands of words to make one point,
what do they aim to clarify?
I urge you to reconsider in detail,
not merely to engage in verbose rhetoric."
A Refutation of the "Natural Love of Learning" Essay in One Piece
The nature of the people is such that
they love peace and hate danger,
they love ease and hate toil.
Therefore, if not disturbed,
their desires are fulfilled;
if not coerced,
their wills are followed.
In the primordial age,
the great simplicity was not yet impaired;
rulers above had no embellishments,
and the people below had no competitions.
All things were complete and principles in order,
everyone naturally content.
When full, they slept peacefully;
when hungry, they sought food;
joyfully filling their bellies,
unaware that this was the age of supreme virtue.
In such a state,
how could they know the beginnings of benevolence and righteousness,
or the formalities of rituals and laws?
But when the true men no longer existed,
and the great Way declined,
only then did they begin to create writings
to convey their ideas.
They distinguished among various things,
grouping them into categories.
They established benevolence and righteousness
to bind people's hearts.
They set up names and duties
to regulate their external conduct.
They encouraged learning and discoursed on culture
to mystify their teachings.
Thus, the Six Classics became tangled,
and the Hundred Schools flourished intensely,
opening the path to honor and profit,
so people rushed forward without realizing it.
Hence, like greedy birds
feeding on the grains in gardens and ponds,
those seeking security
distort their wills to follow customs.
Holding brushes and tablets,
they find enough respite;
accumulating knowledge and understanding the classics,
they replace farming.
Thus, they study only when in distress,
learning to achieve glory;
they practice only after calculation,
and through fondness, practice becomes habit.
It seems natural,
leading you, sir, to call it natural.
Tracing its origin:
the Six Classics aim to restrain and guide,
while human nature finds joy in following desires.
Restraint and guidance go against its wishes,
whereas following desires achieves naturalness.
Thus, the attainment of naturalness
does not come from the restraining Six Classics;
the foundation of preserving nature
does not require rituals and laws that violate emotions.
Therefore, benevolence and righteousness serve artificial principles,
not the essential art of nurturing genuineness;
modesty and yielding arise from contention,
not from what is natural.
From this, it can be said:
birds do not destroy themselves to seek tameness,
nor do beasts form groups to seek domestication;
similarly, the true nature of humans
should naturally indulge in these rituals and learning without coercion.
The argument also states:
Delicious dishes and rare delicacies,
even if never tasted before,
must be delightful when tried,
pleasing to the palate.
Staying in a dark room,
seeing the light of a candle,
one feels joy in the heart without being taught.
How much more so in the darkness of a long night,
to be illuminated by the sun,
emotions stirred and enlightened,
lifting one's blindness.
Even if events arise anew,
emotions respond fundamentally,
it does not harm the natural love of learning.
I counter:
The mouth's response to sweetness and bitterness,
the body's to pain and itch,
react to stimuli and act in response,
without needing to learn first,
nor awaiting borrowing to possess.
This is an inevitable principle,
which I do not dispute.
Now, you use this inevitable principle
to analogize the not-inevitable love of learning,
fearing it may be a specious argument,
where learning is likened to a single grain,
and thus it stands.
Now, you establish the Six Classics as the standard,
uphold benevolence and righteousness as the core,
use rules as your carriage,
and instruction as nourishment;
following this path leads to success,
straying from it to stagnation.
Your mind wanders and eyes gaze intently,
seeing nothing beyond;
racing all year long,
thoughts never leave their place.
Gathering clans to offer opinions,
only learning is valued;
clutching books and picking phrases,
bowing and sighing in admiration,
you embrace these words
as glorious.
Thus, you, sir, call the Six Classics the sun,
and not learning a long night.
But if we consider the hall as a temporary shelter,
recitation as ghostly chatter,
the Six Classics as weeds and filth,
benevolence and righteousness as stench and decay,
seeing texts makes the eyes squint,
practicing courtesies bends the back,
wearing official robes causes cramps,
discussing rituals rots the teeth;
then, abandoning them all
and starting anew with all things,
even if you, sir, love learning tirelessly,
it will still be lacking.
Thus, the previous lack of learning
may not have been a long night,
and the Six Classics may not be the sun.
A proverb says:
A beggar does not insult a horse doctor.
If we encounter the governance of antiquity without writings,
we could gain peace without learning,
achieve aspirations without effort;
then what need for the Six Classics,
what desire for benevolence and righteousness?
From this perspective,
aren't today's learners
first calculating and then learning?
If acting only after calculation,
