it is not a natural response.
Your words,
I fear, are like obtaining pickled calamus.
A Refutation of "There Is No Good or Bad Fortune in Dwellings: On Preserving Life"
The spirits are distant and elusive,
good and bad fortune hard to discern.
Even with average people exhausting themselves,
none can grasp the essence,
and it easily leads to confusion.
Thus, the Master refrained from answering questions in the end,
cautious about the supernatural and silent.
Therefore, the ancients displayed benevolence in things,
hid their usefulness in themselves,
knowing it couldn't be shared by all,
not intentionally concealing it,
but because it wasn't meant to be clarified.
I have no intention of aspiring, yet you, sir, with a self-opinionated and narrow view,
decisively without doubt.
So resolute in judgment,
enough to decide alone.
Reflecting on your discourse,
its main points are mostly illogical.
Carefully, based on your words,
I raise this refutation.
Just as examining metal and wood,
unsure of their place,
none can manage consumption.
The world lacks a self-regulating Way,
and methods have no exclusive goodness.
If not the right person,
the Way does not empty manifest;
rituals, music, governance, and punishments,
constant external affairs,
still have omissions,
let alone the obscure and subtle?
Even if one wishes to clarify the divine and subtle,
dispel confusion,
lift stagnation,
establish foundations
to illuminate the origins;
one must decide and examine the essentials
to have evidence.
If merely gathering the foolish masses,
like silkworm seeds,
angrily discarding them,
and thus claiming there is no principle of yin-yang and good or bad fortune,
isn't it like choking and blaming the grains,
or drowning and blaming the boat and oars?
Discussion states:
A palace built to last a hundred years
cannot make a child who dies young live long;
an inauspicious terrain alignment
cannot cause Péng Zǔ to die prematurely.
It is also said:
Through Xǔ Fù's physiognomy,
the tattooed Marquis of Tiáo and Yīng Bù later became kings—
all were matters of innate fate.
I respond:
This implies that fate is predetermined,
and longevity has its fixed measure.
Disaster cannot be avoided by wisdom,
nor blessings attained through effort.
Yīng Bù feared pain,
yet ultimately suffered execution by saw;
Yà Fū dreaded starvation,
and indeed met with famine's calamity.
All things and events,
every encounter,
are nothing but manifestations of physiognomy and fate.
Yet in the age of Táng and Yú,
why were fates uniformly prolonged?
Among the soldiers at Chángpíng,
why were fates equally brief?
This is what puzzles me.
If we follow this reasoning,
even the cautious like Zēng Shēn and Yán Huí
could not avoid misfortune,
while the wicked like Jié and Zhí
should naturally flourish.
If fortune and misfortune are predetermined,
immutable,
then why did the ancients say, "Families that accumulate good deeds
will have abundant blessings"?
"Practice faithfulness and cherish obedience,
and heaven will protect them"?
If blessings respond only after good is accumulated,
and divine aid comes only after trust is established,
it is like crimes inviting punishment
or merits leading to rewards.
If one must first accumulate [virtue] before receiving retribution,
this follows logical principle
and is not an obscure, passive encounter.
If all is attributed to physiognomy and fate,
this would mean determining fate through actions
and fixing fortune through knowledge and effort—
I fear this contradicts the original argument's intent.
This again is what puzzles me.
It is further said:
If overeating causes indigestion,
one must take digestive pills.
If life span is naturally destined,
why fear overeating?
Why take good medicine?
If taking medicine is part of one's physiognomy,
why is dwelling not the same?
If even with fate,
one still needs medicine for self-preservation,
how do we know physiognomy does not require dwellings for support?
If medicine can be discussed but dwellings cannot,
I fear there may be those in the world who would argue otherwise.
Since it is said that life span cannot be sought,
even more so than nobility or baseness;
yet it is also said that those skilled at seeking longevity
must first know the origins of calamity and illness,
then they can prevent them.
Then is longevity truly attainable?
Or unattainable?
Since it is said that Péng Zǔ's seven hundred years
and the child's early death
are both natural to their innate fate;
yet it is also said that not knowing how to prevent illness
leads to shortened life and premature death.
Seeking substance in emptiness,
thus innate fate is not fulfilled.
This means the coming of longevity or early death
arises from how one uses the body,
and the fulfillment of innate fate
is achieved through skillful seeking.
Then should not those with short lives
be called foolish?
And those with long lives
be called wise?
If longevity and early death result from foolishness or wisdom,
then the theory of natural fate
and its unattainability—
where do they stand?
All these points
reveal contradictions in this elegant discourse.
Discussion states:
Focus the breath to attain softness,
reduce selfishness and desires,
directly follow what suits one's nature,
and align with the proper measures of nurturing life—
seek these within one's bosom,
and they will be attained.
It is also said:
Those skilled at nurturing life
exhaust it in harmony.
How true these words!
Not that I disagree,
but I say preserving life fully is not exhausted in this alone.
Not entering perilous states
avoids the harm of chaotic governance.
Double gates and night watchmen's clappers
guard against violent disasters.
Dwelling must be in elevated, dry places
to keep away the perils of wind and poison.
All external matters that can cause harm—
this is insufficient to cover their full extent.
How can maintaining unity and harmony alone exhaust it?
In focusing on stillness and few desires,
none surpassed Dān Bào, who at seventy
had the complexion of a child,
truly demonstrating the effect of gentleness and harmony.
Yet one day he was eaten by a tiger—
was this not due to relying on the inner while neglecting the outer?
If we say Dān Bào's physiognomy destined him for the kitchen,
and even wisdom could not save him,
then what benefit are few desires?
And how can we say nurturing life is attainable?
If Dān Bào's incomplete perfection led to disaster,
then the way of aiding life
is not limited to unity and harmony.
If harmony alone cannot preserve life,
then among external things that cause harm,
I do not know how to balance them.
Discussion states:
Diviners assessing existing dwellings show efficacy,
but have no proof when creating new ones.
I ask: when divining existing dwellings and finding efficacy,
is it only the walls and house being divined?
Or the occupants' fortune and misfortune?
If divining the occupants reveals prosperity or decline,
this is divining the people,
not the existing dwelling.
If divining the existing dwelling reveals fortune and misfortune,
this means the dwelling itself has good or evil,
and the occupants follow it.
Thus the diviner observes the surface
and discerns the interior.
If the dwelling can control people to follow it,
then those destined for good fortune
would suffer disaster in an unlucky house;
while the rebellious and immoral
would gain blessings in an auspicious residence.
Is the cause of fortune and misfortune
solely the dwelling?
Or also due to the people,
making new dwellings unverifiable?
If fortune and misfortune truly stem from people,
then even with existing dwellings,
how can one claim there is efficacy?
If so,
can it truly be divined?
Or not?
Does the dwelling truly exist?
Or does it not?
Discussion states:
Residential divination is like augury,
it can reveal fortune or misfortune,
but cannot create fortune or misfortune.
Response:
These appear similar but are fundamentally different.
Augury deals with unforeseeable fortunes,
responding to external signs,
portending future omens.
House analysis disregards the occupant's virtue or folly,
observing only established conditions.
What is transmitted
are already formed patterns.
Just as seeing dragon-like features
predicts future nobility,
or observing facial creases
foretells impending hunger.
Each has its causation,
not mere guesswork.
Now observing their shared ability to predict fortunes,
you equate house analysis
with augury without distinction,
like mistaking a qín for a kōnghóu
- not only misunderstanding the qín
but missing both instruments' essence. Even granting your argument
that housing and augury align,
merely knowing without affecting outcomes,
then when fortune is predetermined,
what benefit comes from knowledge?
Whether divining or not
becomes irrelevant;
yet ancients undertaking great deeds
would consult turtle shells for auspicious signs
to determine proper courses -
was this meaningless?
Here lies my doubt.
King Wǔ planning Zhōu's capital
declared "the king consulted oracles"
to establish Hàojīng;
Duke of Zhōu relocating cities
divined between Jiàn and Chán rivers,
finally choosing Luò for sustenance.
Furthermore:
"Divined the burial site for interment"
- our ancestors practiced this
with such reverence;
you now reject it
with present arguments.
Who should we trust?
Discussion states:
Providing a ministerial residence
won't turn commoners into ministers -
this proves my point.
Counterargument:
Commoners cannot long inhabit noble residences.
Does this mean residences lack influence?
Response:
Not that auspicious dwellings
solely bring blessings,
but that virtuous persons
combining personal excellence
with divined residences,
accumulating goodness through conduct,
achieve supreme fortune.
Like skilled farmers
possessing cultivation arts
yet selecting fertile land,
enhancing it through labor,
gaining full granaries.
Seeing commoners fail to prosper in good residences
and declaring dwellings neutral
resembles dismissing soil quality
after seeing poor harvests
from inept farming.
Fertile land alone
cannot grow crops;
auspicious residences alone
cannot create fortune.
Their interdependent principle confirmed,
housing fortune becomes undeniable.
Now trusting omens
abandons human reason;
clinging to divination
neglects cosmic harmony;
relying solely on intellect
forgets celestial principles.
This resembles recognizing rain nourishes life
then idly awaiting harvest
without cultivation.
Hence doubts arise,
biased views emerge,
differing perspectives
fail to integrate.
Those embracing both aspects
might partially misunderstand dwellings.
Discussion states:
Date taboos and exorcisms
were avoided by wise kings,
favored by declining rulers.
This sounds reasonable
but isn't entirely accurate.
Tāng praying at Sānglín,
Duke of Zhōu holding jade tablets -
were these not exorcisms?
"The auspicious day being Wù"
with prayers and sacrifices -
were these not date selections?
These originate from your school's

The Grand Preceptor's Admonition
Vast is the Primordial Simplicity,
Where yang shines and yin congeals.
The Two Molds shape creation,
And human relations begin to flourish.
In the beginning, all was obscure and dark,
Without worries or schemes.
Desires arose with the emergence of things,
Troubles formed through events.
Offending mechanisms and touching harms,
Wisdom could not save lives.
Honoring elders and returning to benevolence
Is the natural disposition.
Thus, the way of the ruler is natural,
Necessarily entrusted to the wise and enlightened.
In the remote past, vast and boundless,
None were without peace.
After Héxū passed away,
Huángxī carried on.
Silent and tranquil, without adornment,
The Great Simplicity remained intact.
All things were harmonious and joyful,
Neither dying prematurely nor separating.
Then came Táng and Yú,
Still upholding this legacy.
Their substance was simple and uncomplicated,
Responding to Heaven and following its rules.
They wore coarse cloth for garments,
And lived in earthen and wooden dwellings.
If anything lost its nature,
They feared as if it were their own fault.
Consulting widely to promote prosperity,
They finally abdicated to Shùn and Yǔ.
Those who govern toil,
While those who look up to them rest.
The perfect man values his person,
And abandons rule without regret.
Thus, Zǐzhōu pleaded illness,
Shíhù took to the raft;
Xǔyóu bowed respectfully,
Declining rule over the nine provinces.
The ancient kings, benevolent and loving,
Pitying the age and worrying for the times;
Grieving that all things were declining,
Only then did they assume rule.
Later, when virtue decayed,
The Great Way sank into obscurity.
Wisdom was used daily,
Gradually favoring one's own kin.
Fearing that things would fall into discord,
They rolled up their sleeves and established benevolence.
Cunning for profit grew more competitive,
Elaborate rites were repeatedly displayed.
Punishments and teachings vied in application,
Innate nature was lost and truth perished.
In the declining age, morals deteriorated,
Successors inherited power and resources.
Relying on prestige and depending on influence,
They neither befriended nor learned from others.
They carved up the world,
To serve their private interests.
Thus, the ruler's position became more extravagant,
And ministers harbored ambitious thoughts.
Exhausting their wisdom to scheme for the state,
They did not hesitate to reduce it to ashes.
Though rewards and punishments existed,
They neither encouraged nor restrained.
If then, arrogant and full of themselves, they indulged their whims,
Amassing troops and seizing power arbitrarily.
Flaunting their might and unleashing cruelty,
Disasters piled up like mountains.
Punishment was originally meant to curb violence,
But now it is used to intimidate the virtuous.
Once it was for the sake of the world,
Now it is for the sake of oneself.
The people resent their superiors,
The ruler suspects his ministers.
Chaos and ruin abound,
And the state falls into collapse.
Thus, Yīn Xīn, being unprincipled,
First hung on the plain banner;
The Zhōu dynasty, abandoning measure,
Plotted against the boar-keeper.
Chǔ Líng, extreme in tyranny,
Faced rebellion at Gānxī;
Jìn Lì, cruel and oppressive,
Provoked Luán Shū to revolt.
Zhǔfù discarded the rites,
Sparing not even the unhatched eggs;
Qín Shǐhuáng, brutal and poisonous,
Brought calamity flowing to the four seas.
Hence, fallen states follow one another,
From ancient to modern times, a continuous succession.
Despising those destroyed,
Yet inheriting their signs of doom.
At first, secure as a mountain,
Later, collapsing in ruin.
Facing the blade and shaking the spear,
What gain is there in regret?
Therefore, those who occupy the imperial throne,
Do not say, "I am exalted,"
And neglect your virtuous reputation;
Do not say, "I am strong,"
And indulge in arrogance and excess.
Reject those flatterers and favorites,
Admit instead those who offer candid counsel.
Sycophantic words please the ear,
But taint virtue and breed calamity.
Oh, myriad beings,
I appeal to you and make my declaration.
Appoint only the worthy,
Why must they be relatives?
Compliance creates harmony,
And the people will indeed emulate it.
The root of order and chaos,
Is there no way to promote enlightenment?
Majestic Son of Heaven,
Reflect and inquire into your faults.
Guide others with an open mind,
Sincerely seeking honest words.
Your minister, in charge of instruction,
Dares to admonish you from the forefront.

not truly human.
However, a noble person applies their mind,
desiring to act according to standards,
naturally appropriate.

they must deliberate before taking action.
If it is where their aspiration leads,
then their mouth and heart pledge in unison,
remaining steadfast unto death without wavering.

aiming for certain success.

or drawn by external temptations,
or burdened by inner desires;
unable to endure immediate hardships,
or unable to bear minor emotions,
then they debate whether to advance or retreat.

leads to inner conflict.
Inner conflict,
causes the emotions that once controlled them to prevail.

others fail before achieving even a single basket's worth.
In defense, they are not firm;
in attack, they are timid and weak.
When making vows, they often break them;
when consulting on plans, they easily leak secrets.
Facing pleasure, they indulge recklessly;
in comfort, they act without restraint.

they achieve no fruitful merit;
despite a year's diligence,
they have not a day's accomplishment.
This is why the noble sigh in regret.

Yí Qí's complete purity,
Zhǎn Jì's unwavering faith,
Sū Wǔ's preservation of integrity,
they can be called resolute.
Thus, they guard it with effortless ease,
and embody it,
as if by nature.
This is the pinnacle of upholding aspiration.
Regarding the officials in charge,
one should merely respect them,
not become overly intimate,
nor visit frequently,
visits should be timely.
When among the crowd,
one should not lag behind alone,
nor stay overnight.

officials enjoy inquiring about external affairs,
and if they sometimes act on reports,
those resentful will say it was someone's tale,
leaving no way to exonerate oneself.
Act broadly, speak sparingly,
be cautious and self-guarding,
then the path to blame and resentment dissolves.
One's conduct should be pure and aloof.
If faced with burdensome tasks,
where others expect full commitment,
or entrust requests,
one should humbly decline,
stating one never involves in such matters,
and they should understand.
If there is urgent plea,
hard to bear in heart,
one may outwardly refuse,
but secretly assist.
The reason being,
above, to avoid the risks of undue compliance,
in the middle, to cut off excessive demands from common folk,
below, to preserve an unsullied reputation of integrity;
this is another aspect of upholding aspiration.
In all actions, first assess their feasibility;
if appropriate,
proceed with it,
but if others wish to change it,
explain why it should be altered.
If their argument is excellent,
do not feel ashamed to yield and persist in error;
if their reasoning is insufficient,
and they press with emotional appeals to hold firm.
Even if they persist,
stand firmly by your position,
this is another facet of upholding aspiration.
Do not engage in petty displays of integrity,
but if encountering poverty and need,
and able to provide relief,
act righteously upon seeing it.
If someone makes a request of you,
first reflect inwardly;
if the cost is great,
and the righteous aid provided is small,
weigh the priorities and refuse.
Even if pressured persistently,
still cut it off.
Generally, when people ask for help,
it's because they lack what I have,
hence they seek from me,
this means giving them much.
If unaware of this,
and lightly exhaust oneself,
unable to refuse face-to-face,
forcing to meet minor sentiments,
is not having aspiration.
Speech,
is the mechanism of a noble person,
when the mechanism moves, responses follow,
then the form of right and wrong becomes clear.
Thus, one must be cautious.
If the meaning is not well understood,
and one intends to speak,
then fear the risk of misunderstanding,
and temporarily endure it.
Later, reflecting on not speaking of it,
finding no other issue,
then the earlier speech might have been inappropriate;
thus, being able not to speak,
fully achieves appropriateness.
Moreover, common people spread good news slowly but bad news quickly,
and enjoy discussing others' faults,
this is the talk of ordinary folk.
What is said in gatherings,
unless lofty discourse,
but mere news and gossip,
minor agreements and disagreements,
one should regard it highly but distantly,
not necessary to respond.
Speak only what is righteous,
be calm and reverent to the Way,
is this not called having few regrets?
When people argue with each other,
and the merits are unclear,
be careful not to get involved.
Instead, silently observe,
their right and wrong will naturally appear.
If there's minor right not worth affirming,
or minor wrong not worth condemning,
ultimately, one can refrain from speaking and wait.
Even if asked,
still plead ignorance.
Similar with recent discussions.
If at a drinking gathering,
you see people arguing,
and the situation seems to escalate,
simply leave without ado.
This is a sign of impending conflict.
Staying to watch will reveal right and wrong,
and siding inevitably leads to taking sides,
speaking up will favor one party,
the one in the wrong,
will think themselves right,
and assume the one calling them wrong is biased,
thus breeding resentment and malice;
or one might face offensive words,
even if observing impartially,
clearly seeing the rights and wrongs,
the dispute remains unresolved,
then benevolence without firmness,
holds no righteousness,
so it's best to avoid it.
Generally, those who argue and sue,
are petty people.
Even if there is right and wrong,
engaging in their chaos,
even winning, is it praiseworthy?
If unable to avoid, getting drunk is better.
If there's something you wish to keep private,
and they insist on knowing,
if they press relentlessly,
or coerce with base emotions,
do not fear these insignificant individuals,
and be swayed by them.
Leading to full disclosure.
Now, firmly state,
not knowing, not recognizing,
is truly having aspiration,
unless they are old friends or neighbors,
or close acquaintances below that,
if they invite you,
decline with other reasons,
and do not go.
Detached from glory and wealth, one has fewer desires,
unless extremely urgent,
never seek or desire,
this is the highest virtue.
No need for petty humility,
practice great magnanimity;
no need for minor shows of integrity,
uphold great yielding.
Like declining office at court,
or yielding one's life in righteousness,
as Kǒng Wénrǎng sought to die in his brother's place,
this is the integrity of loyal officials and martyrs.
All people have public and private matters,
be careful not to force knowing what others know.
They know I know it,
then they will hold grudges against me.
Now if one knows but does not speak,
that is tantamount to ignorance.
If you see people whispering in private discussions,
immediately leave and rise,
so as not to provoke their resentment.
Sometimes under pressure,
they forcibly engage me in conversation.
If their words are wicked and dangerous,
then one should sternly correct them with righteousness and moral principles.
Why?
Because a noble person does not tolerate hypocritical and shallow words.
Once matters fail,
they will say that so-and-so previously knew about my affairs,
hence one should be deeply prepared for this.
When people speak privately,
there is nothing they won't discuss,
so one ought to be mindful in advance.
Why does one flee upon seeing such conversations?
Perhaps by chance learning of their private matters,
if in agreement, it may be acceptable,
but if not, then they fear the affair will be exposed,
and think to harm others to erase traces.
Those not sincerely admired,
yet come to tease and mock,
laughing at people's flaws—
simply do not comply or join in their frivolity,
gradually leading to non-participation;
and do not become overly cold or arrogant,
but rather tend to respond with silence.
The situation cannot last long,
and it will naturally cease.
Unless under one's supervision,
and there is no other appropriate interaction,
if there is the intent of sharing wine,
or the goodwill of modest gifts,
these are common in human relations,
and need not be rejected.
Beyond this,
unless there is profound harmony.
Gifts of silk and cloth,
presents of carriages and robes,
should be deeply refused.
Why?
Ordinary people often belittle righteousness and value profit,
now those who exhaust themselves for you,
must have motives and act for gain,
offering goods to curry favor and seek repayment—
these are what vulgar people gladly accept,
but what noble people greatly detest.
■■■■■■■ also confused,
no need to force or drag,
strongly urging others to drink.
If not drinking, let it be,
if others come to persuade,
one should hold the cup for them,
neither mocking nor refusing.
When seeing them drunk and tipsy, stop,
carefully not reaching the point of exhaustion and drunkenness,
unable to control oneself.
Four-Character Poem
Drifting white clouds,
follow the wind and circle back;
deep green waters,
fill the hollows and overflow.
Riding the current far away,
to the orchid-covered bend by myself.
Staff in hand, responding to all,
embracing it in my pure heart.
A long whistle in the clear wilderness,
only to tell of sorrow.
Soaring high, the graceful luan bird,
spreads its wings in the great clarity;
looking down upon the purple stars,
gazing up at the plain courtyard.
Treading the mysterious void,
floating and sinking without form.
About to wander beyond the realm,
whistling to companions with long cries.
The spirit □ not present,
who will journey alone?
There is a boat floating and capsizing,
held by the towline and reins.
Oars of juniper, paddles of pine,
as if with dragon's subtlety.
□ crossing perilous fords,
passing the ferry, not returning.
Thinking of friends in the deep woods,
embracing simplicity by the mountain's edge.
Guarding the vessel, devoted to the task,
unable to soar high.
Feathered ascent to Huàyuè,
transcending to roam the clear skies.
Canopies of clouds fluttering gently,
six dragons drifting gracefully.
Left, wearing pepper and cassia,
right, adorned with orchid shoots.
Ascending the sunny path with praise,
Prince Wángzǐ offers the carriage.
Lovely famous mountains,
where the true men reside.
Harmonizing things and nurturing life,
wandering freely with the Dào.
Three Five-Character Poems
Human life is like the morning dew,
worldly changes full of numerous snares.
If there must be an ultimate end,
then Péng Zǔ and Lǎo Dān are not excessive.
Benevolence and righteousness dilute pure simplicity,
foresight loses the splendor of the Dào.
Lingering weakness loses nature,
innocence is hard to harmonize.
The man of Yǐng recognized artisan Shí,
Zhōngzǐ knew Bóyá;
true men are not often present,
who will join in the lofty song?
In the long night, home in inaction,
walking alone by the bright courtyard's side.
Raising my head to see the celestial path,
flowing light illuminates the eight poles.
Holding my heart, mourning the decadent age,
longing for the great Dào felt pressing.
Frivolous are the scholars in power,
endlessly advancing through thorns.
Gain and loss come on their own,
honor and disgrace consume each other.
Vermilion and purple, though dark and yellow,
the primordial simplicity values colorlessness.
Profound and serene, embodying the ultimate Dào,
transformation of forms shares the same ebb and flow.
Vulgar people are not to be befriended,
one may neighbor with Sōng and Qiáo.
Why stay in the filthy and turbid world,
swaying and increasing the dust of defilement?
Resolute, I journey far,
preparing the carriage, awaiting the auspicious hour.
Lightly rising, soaring beyond the realm,
washing wings at the Fúsāng shore.
Wandering and playing on the divine peak,
playing the qin, singing of the great truth.
Cleansing the five organs in the dark waters,
transformation sudden as if divine.
Cháng'é offers wondrous medicine,
feathers gather, radiant and new.
Once soaring from Kāiyáng,
looking down upon those on the road.
Alas, people of the world,
how can this place long sustain your being?
Poem on Roaming as an Immortal
Gracefully, the phoenix carriage,
encounters this net of snares.

Ode to the Qín
Admirable, my elegant instrument,
born of the spirit mountain's unhewn jade.
Its form embodies virtuous truth,
pure, harmonious, and natural.
Bathed in spring snow,
serene as a cave spring.
Warm as benevolence itself,
jade-moistened, radiant externally.
In ancient times of Huángdì and Shénnóng,
this divine object arrived.
Majestic was Chónghuà,
who entrusted his heart to the five strings.
Repelling evil, embracing righteousness,
tirelessly, like an immortal.
Harmonizing and nurturing the spirit,
thus ensuring long life.
